listening.script:
Narrator: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a leisure centre to ask about membership. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 7.
Agent: Good morning, Riverside Leisure Centre. How can I help you?
Caller: Oh, hello. I'm thinking of joining the centre, and I wondered if you could tell me a bit about membership.
Agent: Of course. I can take a few details now and explain the options as we go. Could I have your name, please?
Caller: Yes, it's Jessica Delaney.
Agent: And could you spell your surname for me?
Caller: Certainly. D, E, L, A, N, E, Y.
Agent: Thank you. And your address?
Caller: It's fourteen Marlowe Road. That's M, A, R, L, O, W, E.
Agent: Fourteen Marlowe Road. Lovely, that's only about ten minutes from here. Now, we have three types of membership. Full membership is thirty-nine pounds a month, and you can come in at any time we're open.
Caller: Right.
Agent: Then there's off-peak membership. That's cheaper, thirty-four pounds a month, but you can only use the centre before four o'clock on weekdays. At weekends you can come whenever you like.
Caller: I work from home, so I can usually get away during the day. Off-peak sounds ideal.
Agent: Great. And there's a family package too, but I don't think you need that.
Caller: No, it's just me.
Agent: So, off-peak at thirty-four pounds. And what are you mainly interested in doing here?
Caller: Well, I used to play a lot of tennis, but my knee isn't what it was, and my doctor told me to try something gentler. A friend of mine recommended pilates, so that's what I'd like to start with.
Agent: We have pilates classes every weekday morning, so that works well with off-peak. We've also just opened a climbing wall, if you ever fancy a challenge.
Caller: Maybe one day! Pilates first, I think.
Agent: And when would you like your membership to start?
Caller: I'm away until the end of February, so could I start on the first of March?
Agent: Ah, I'm afraid we're closed on the first and second of March for our annual maintenance. The pool is drained and cleaned. Would the third suit you?
Caller: Yes, the third of March is fine.
Agent: Lovely. And may I ask how you heard about us? Was it through our website?
Caller: No, actually. My neighbour did mention you, but it was an advert in the local newspaper that made me pick up the phone.
Agent: That's useful to know, thank you.
Narrator: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 8 to 10.
Agent: Now, a few practical things. Will you be driving here?
Caller: Probably, yes.
Agent: The car park at the front of the building fills up very quickly in the mornings. But there's a much bigger one behind the main building, and members can park there free of charge, so I'd use that one.
Caller: Good to know.
Agent: All new members also have a short induction before they use the gym or join a class. Normally those take place on Wednesday evenings, but of course with off-peak membership you can't come in after four on a weekday.
Caller: Oh, that's a problem.
Agent: Not at all. We run a session on Saturday mornings as well, so I'll book you onto that one instead.
Caller: Perfect.
Agent: And when you come in for the first time, please bring a bank statement or a utility bill, something that shows your address. We take the photo for your membership card here at reception, so you don't need to bring one. And you'd only need a note from your doctor if you'd had an operation in the last six months.
Caller: That's fine. I'll dig out a bill. Thank you so much for your help.
Narrator: That is the end of Part 1.

listening.script:
Narrator: Part 2. You will hear a manager talking to a group of new volunteers at a nature reserve. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
Guide: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Ashcombe Wetland Reserve. My name's Claire, and I coordinate the volunteer programme here. Before we head outside, I'd like to give you a bit of background and explain what you'll be doing.
Guide: Many visitors assume the reserve was created to protect the bitterns that nest in our reed beds, and they are certainly our most famous residents. But in fact the lakes you'll see were dug in the nineteen sixties as reservoirs, to store drinking water for the city. When the water company built a larger reservoir further north, these lakes were no longer needed, and over time the birds moved in. The reserve itself was only established about thirty years ago.
Guide: People are often surprised to hear that winter, not summer, is when we see the most visitors. That's because tens of thousands of ducks and geese arrive from the Arctic, and it's quite a spectacle. Two years ago we introduced parking charges, and there were fears that numbers would drop, but they've held steady. And the café, which opened last spring, has been very popular with regular visitors, although it hasn't really brought in new ones.
Guide: Now, I know some of you are keen to lead guided walks, and that's wonderful. But nobody leads a walk until they've been with us for at least three months. On your first day, each of you will be paired with one of our long-standing volunteers, and you'll simply work alongside them and learn how things are done. You'll have your safety briefing this morning, so that's out of the way before you start.
Guide: One of our ongoing challenges is the boardwalk that crosses the marsh. It was widened last year so that wheelchairs and pushchairs can pass each other, and apart from bank holidays it rarely gets crowded. The real problem is that the winter floods lift the planks out of place, so it needs constant repairs, and that's something volunteers often help with.
Guide: Finally, if you spot a rare bird, we'd love to know about it. We used to keep a logbook in the visitor centre, and some people still write in it out of habit, but please record sightings on the reserve's phone app instead. The warden checks it every evening, and it means the information reaches our national database straight away.
Narrator: Now look at questions 16 to 20.
Guide: Let me show you on the map where the main volunteer jobs are. Up here at the top is the North Hide. It's the best place for watching waders, and it's where volunteers refill the bird feeders every morning. Years ago, tickets were sold from a hut beside it, but that's all done online now.
Guide: Just south of that is Willow Pond. This is where school groups come for pond-dipping, catching small creatures in nets to look at them, and our volunteers help to run the children's activities there.
Guide: To the east are the Reed Beds. These are important for filtering the water that flows into the lakes, so once a week volunteers collect water samples there and test them for pollution.
Guide: In the south-west corner is the Meadow. It's covered in wild flowers in early summer, and visitors are always asking what they are, so volunteers stationed there help people identify the different plants. You won't need to pick up litter there, by the way; since we removed the bins, people take their rubbish home.
Guide: And finally, by the main gate, there's the Old Pump House. It's a lovely Victorian building, and it's now the meeting point for our evening bat walks, which volunteers help to guide in the summer months.
Narrator: That is the end of Part 2.

listening.scriptTitle: A research project on food waste
listening.script:
Narrator: Part 3. You will hear two students, Maya and Daniel, discussing their research project on food waste with their tutor. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.
Tutor: Come in, both of you. So, how's the food waste project going?
Maya: Pretty well, I think. We've finished collecting the data.
Tutor: Good. Remind me why you chose this topic. I seem to remember suggesting transport.
Daniel: You did, but we'd already got the idea from our own kitchen in halls. The amount of food people threw away every week was shocking, so we wanted to find out how typical it was.
Tutor: And there isn't a great deal of research on students specifically, so that's a good gap to fill.
Maya: Exactly.
Tutor: How did the questionnaire go?
Maya: Better than expected in terms of numbers. We got over two hundred responses, and it only took about five minutes to fill in, so people didn't give up halfway.
Daniel: The trouble was question five, where we asked people to estimate how many portions they wasted each week. It turned out people understood portion in completely different ways. Some meant a whole meal, others a single slice of bread.
Tutor: That's a common issue. You'll need to discuss that in your limitations section. What about the photographs?
Daniel: We photographed the kitchen bins in three halls every evening for two weeks.
Tutor: I thought that was a clever idea. It gives you far more reliable data than asking people to remember what they've thrown away. And as long as no names or faces appear, I don't think privacy is a concern.
Maya: That's a relief.
Tutor: Did anything in the results surprise you?
Maya: Well, we predicted that waste would go up before exams, when people are stressed and order takeaways, and it did. But we also assumed that students who cook more often would waste more, because they buy more fresh food. In fact it was the opposite. The regular cooks wasted much less.
Tutor: Interesting. Perhaps they plan their shopping better. So what's next? You could compare your findings with another university.
Daniel: We did think about that, but we really don't have time this term. We're going to interview the managers of the halls instead, to find out what they've tried in the past.
Tutor: That sounds sensible.
Narrator: Now look at questions 26 to 30.
Tutor: Let's go through your draft report section by section. The introduction?
Maya: I know, it's far too long. It's nearly three pages.
Tutor: Yes, I'd cut it to one page at most. Get to your research question quickly.
Daniel: The literature review is quite short.
Tutor: Short is fine, but you only cite four studies. You really need to find more sources than that. The library database should help.
Maya: For the methods, we explained everything in words, but it's quite hard to follow.
Tutor: A simple flow chart showing the stages of your data collection would make it much clearer. Your headings are fine, though.
Daniel: And the results section has all our tables in it.
Tutor: It's too detailed for the main text. Keep a summary table there and move the full tables to an appendix at the end.
Maya: What about the recommendations?
Tutor: Those are basically done. Just check them carefully for typing errors.
Narrator: That is the end of Part 3.

listening.script:
Narrator: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about urban heat islands. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
Lecturer: Good afternoon. Today I'm going to talk about a phenomenon that affects almost every large city on the planet, the urban heat island. Simply put, this is the tendency of cities to be significantly warmer than the countryside around them. I'll look at the causes first, then the effects, and finally at what cities are doing about it.
Lecturer: So, what causes it? The first factor is the materials cities are built from. Dark surfaces, and asphalt in particular, absorb a great deal of the sun's energy during the day and then release it slowly as heat at night. Concrete and brick do this too, but asphalt roads and car parks are the worst offenders.
Lecturer: The second factor is the lack of vegetation. Trees and plants cool the air around them through a process called evapotranspiration, which is essentially plants releasing water vapour, rather like sweating. In a typical city centre, there simply isn't enough greenery for this cooling effect to make much difference.
Lecturer: Thirdly, cities generate their own heat. Factories, air-conditioning units and, above all, traffic release enormous amounts of waste heat. In some city centres, heat from traffic alone can raise temperatures by a measurable amount on a still day.
Lecturer: Now, the effects. The difference between city and countryside is usually greatest at night. On calm, clear nights, a city centre can be as much as twelve degrees warmer than nearby rural areas. During heatwaves, this means the city never really cools down.
Lecturer: One obvious consequence is that demand for electricity rises sharply, as people run air conditioners and fans, and this can put serious pressure on power networks during the summer. But the most serious effects are on health. Heat-related illness rises in cities during heatwaves, and the elderly are at the greatest risk, particularly those who live alone. Young children are also vulnerable, but studies consistently show the highest death rates among older people.
Lecturer: So what can be done? One of the simplest measures is the so-called cool roof. Painting roofs white means they reflect sunlight rather than absorbing it. In some trials, white roofs were up to thirty degrees cooler on their surface than dark ones, which significantly reduces the temperature inside the building.
Lecturer: Planting is another obvious solution. A particularly impressive example comes from the Colombian city of Medellín, which created a network of what it calls green corridors. These are streets and waterways planted with trees and shrubs, linking parks across the city. Within a few years, temperatures along these routes had fallen by around two degrees.
Lecturer: A third approach involves the ground itself. Instead of ordinary asphalt, some cities are now using permeable paving, which allows rainwater to soak into the ground. That water then evaporates on hot days and cools the surface, and as a bonus it reduces flooding.
Lecturer: Finally, there's the question of planning. When new districts are designed, architects can take account of the direction of the wind. If streets are aligned so that the wind can flow through them, rather than being blocked by tall buildings, heat is carried away much more efficiently. This costs very little if it's considered from the start, but it's almost impossible to change afterwards.
Narrator: That is the end of Part 4.

reading.passage:
For most of human history, producing more food has meant clearing more land. Forests were cut down, wetlands drained and grasslands ploughed. Today, however, there is little suitable land left to convert, and by 2050 the world's population is expected to approach ten billion, two thirds of whom will live in cities. One proposed answer is vertical farming: growing crops in stacked layers inside buildings, often in the heart of the city.

The idea was popularised by Dickson Despommier, a professor of public health at Columbia University. In 1999 he challenged his students to work out how much food could be grown on the rooftops of New York. Disappointed to find that the answer was very little, the class went on to design an entire skyscraper devoted to farming, which they calculated could feed around 50,000 people. Despommier spent much of the following decade promoting the concept.

Most vertical farms today rely on hydroponics, in which plants grow without soil, their roots sitting in water to which nutrients have been added. A smaller number use aeroponics, where the roots hang in the air and are sprayed at regular intervals with a fine mist. In place of the sun, LED lamps provide light, and these can be tuned to the red and blue wavelengths that plants use most efficiently for photosynthesis. Sensors constantly monitor temperature, humidity and carbon dioxide levels, and adjust them automatically. Because conditions never change with the seasons, crops can be harvested all year round. A lettuce that takes around sixty days to mature in a field may be ready in thirty.

Supporters point to a range of benefits. Because water is collected and recirculated rather than draining away, vertical farms can use up to 95 per cent less water than conventional agriculture. Pests are kept out of the sealed growing rooms, so pesticides are unnecessary. And because the food is grown close to the people who eat it, it spends far less time in lorries and warehouses, arriving fresher and with less waste along the way.

The most serious obstacle is energy. Replacing free sunlight with electric light is expensive, and the electricity needed for lighting is by far the largest operating cost of most vertical farms. This is the main reason they concentrate on leafy greens and herbs, which grow quickly, are light to transport and sell at relatively high prices. Staple crops such as wheat and rice, which need far more light and are sold cheaply, remain completely uneconomic. One study estimated that growing wheat indoors would cost hundreds of times more than growing it in a field. High start-up costs are a further problem, and in recent years a number of well-funded vertical farming companies have gone out of business.

The environmental case is also less clear-cut than it first appears. The carbon footprint of an indoor farm depends heavily on where its electricity comes from. In a country that relies mainly on coal, a lettuce grown in a vertical farm may have a larger carbon footprint than one grown in an open field and transported hundreds of kilometres. Supporters respond that as more electricity is generated from renewable sources, this disadvantage will shrink.

Despite these difficulties, some governments see vertical farming as part of their long-term plans. Singapore, which imports more than 90 per cent of its food, has set a target of producing 30 per cent of its nutritional needs locally by 2030, and indoor farms are expected to make an important contribution. Desert states in the Middle East, where water is scarce, have shown similar interest. Meanwhile, plant scientists are developing compact varieties of fruit and vegetables designed to thrive under artificial light. Vertical farming is unlikely ever to replace traditional agriculture, but it may become a valuable addition to it.

reading.passageTitle: The Bicycle: A Machine That Changed Society
reading.passage:
A  In 1815, the eruption of Mount Tambora in Indonesia threw so much ash into the atmosphere that much of Europe experienced what became known as the year without a summer. Crops failed, and the price of oats soared. Horses, which consumed large quantities of oats, became extremely expensive to keep, and many were slaughtered. It was in this context that a German civil servant, Karl von Drais, built his Laufmaschine, or running machine, in 1817. It had two wooden wheels and a seat, but no pedals: the rider pushed it along with his feet. Von Drais intended it as a cheap alternative to the horse for short journeys, and for a brief period it became fashionable in several European cities.

B  The next major step came in the 1860s in France, when pedals were attached directly to the front wheel. The new machines, known in English as velocipedes, could reach far higher speeds than the running machine. However, they had heavy iron frames and wooden wheels with iron rims, and on the cobbled streets of the time the ride was so jarring that they earned the nickname boneshakers. They were an improvement, but hardly a comfortable one.

C  Because the pedals turned the front wheel directly, the only way to make a bicycle go faster was to make that wheel bigger, so that each turn of the pedals carried the rider further. By the 1870s, front wheels had grown to as much as one and a half metres in diameter, with a tiny wheel at the back, a design later called the penny-farthing. It was fast, but extremely dangerous. The rider sat high above the front wheel, and hitting a stone or a hole could throw him head first over the handlebars. Riding one was largely the pastime of daring young men who could afford both the machine and the risk.

D  The solution arrived in 1885, when the English inventor John Kemp Starley produced the Rover. It had two wheels of similar size and a chain that drove the rear wheel, allowing gears to provide speed without an enormous front wheel. Three years later, John Boyd Dunlop developed the pneumatic tyre, filled with air, which absorbed much of the shock of rough roads. The so-called safety bicycle was comfortable, stable and suitable for almost anyone, and its basic layout has hardly changed since. By the 1890s, a cycling boom was under way in Europe and North America.

E  The consequences went far beyond transport. For women in particular, the bicycle offered a degree of independence that had previously been unthinkable. Cycling in long, heavy skirts was impractical, and the bicycle helped popularise so-called rational dress, including loose trousers known as bloomers. Campaigners for women's rights praised the bicycle as a powerful force for freedom. The bicycle also widened the circle of people that young men and women met. Geneticists studying rural England have found that after the 1890s, people increasingly married partners from neighbouring villages rather than their own, a change some researchers link to the new freedom of movement that cycling provided.

F  In the twentieth century, cycling declined in many countries once falling prices put the motor car within reach of ordinary families. In recent decades, however, it has enjoyed a remarkable revival, especially in cities. Copenhagen and Amsterdam have invested heavily in separated cycle lanes and bridges, and bike-sharing schemes now operate in hundreds of cities worldwide. Governments promote cycling as a way to improve public health, ease congestion and cut the emissions that contribute to climate change. Two centuries after von Drais pushed his running machine through the streets, his invention looks as relevant as ever.

reading.passageTitle: Is Willpower Really a Limited Resource?
reading.passage:
Every day, each of us makes a remarkable number of decisions, from what to eat for breakfast to how to reply to a difficult email. According to a theory that has become hugely popular over the past two decades, this constant decision-making comes at a cost. The idea, known as decision fatigue, holds that the quality of our choices deteriorates after a long session of making them. It grew out of a broader theory proposed by the psychologist Roy Baumeister, who argued that self-control draws on a limited store of mental energy. Like a muscle, he suggested, willpower becomes tired with use, a state he called ego depletion.

The most famous evidence for decision fatigue came from a 2011 study of judges in Israel who were deciding whether prisoners should be released on parole. The researchers found that at the start of each session, judges granted parole in about 65 per cent of cases. As the session went on, the rate fell steadily, sometimes to almost zero, before jumping back up after the judges had taken a break for a meal. The study was reported around the world and has been cited thousands of times, in academic papers, business books and newspaper articles, as proof that tired minds make harsher decisions.

Yet the study has attracted serious criticism. Other researchers pointed out that the order of cases was not random. Prisoners without a lawyer, whose applications were less likely to succeed, tended to be scheduled at the end of each session, which alone could explain much of the pattern. Critics also noted that the effect was implausibly large. If hunger and fatigue really changed judgements this dramatically, they argued, we would see their influence everywhere, in exam marking, medical diagnoses and job interviews, and organisations would have learned to schedule around it long ago. An effect of that size, one statistician remarked, is not so much surprising as unbelievable. I find it hard to disagree.

The broader theory of ego depletion has fared little better. In 2016, a large replication project involving 23 laboratories and more than 2,000 participants tested one of the standard ego depletion experiments. The combined result showed an effect close to zero. Further studies have produced mixed results, and the debate continues. One intriguing line of research suggests that what people believe about willpower may matter more than willpower itself. In experiments by Veronika Job and her colleagues, participants who believed that willpower is easily used up showed signs of depletion after a demanding task, whereas those who believed that mental effort can be energising showed little or no decline.

Another casualty has been the so-called glucose hypothesis, the claim that self-control is fuelled by blood sugar and can be restored with a sugary drink. Early experiments appeared to support it, but later work found that the brain's consumption of glucose barely changes during difficult mental tasks, and that even rinsing the mouth with a sugary drink, without swallowing it, can improve performance, suggesting that the effect works through motivation rather than fuel.

None of this has stopped the idea from spreading into everyday advice. Productivity guides recommend making important decisions early in the morning, and much has been made of former US president Barack Obama's habit of wearing only grey or blue suits so that he had fewer trivial choices to make. Such routines are harmless enough, and they may well be helpful, if only because they save time. But the scientific case for them is far weaker than their popularity suggests.

What, then, should we make of the experience of mental tiredness, which is real enough? A growing number of researchers argue that it is better understood in terms of motivation and attention than as a fuel tank running empty. On this view, after a long period of effort, the mind becomes less willing, rather than less able, to keep going, and our attention shifts towards more rewarding activities. Breaks help not because they refill a store of energy, but because they restore our interest in the task. It is a less tidy story than the one we were told, but it is probably closer to the truth.

listening.script:
Narrator: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a company that organises cycling tours. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.
Agent: Good afternoon, Green Wheels Cycling Tours, Hannah speaking.
Caller: Hello. I'd like to book a guided bike tour for a group of friends, please.
Agent: Certainly. Let me take some details. What name is the booking under?
Caller: Mark Fenwick. That's F, E, N, W, I, C, K.
Agent: Thank you, Mr Fenwick. And how many people will there be in your group?
Caller: Well, originally there were seven of us, but one person has had to drop out, so it'll be six.
Agent: Six people. And which date were you thinking of?
Caller: Saturday the fourteenth of August. Oh, hang on, no. The fourteenth is my sister's wedding. It'll have to be Sunday the fifteenth.
Agent: The fifteenth of August, that's fine, we still have space. Now, will you need us to provide the bikes?
Caller: Yes, please. We were wondering about electric bikes, but most of the group are quite fit, so we'd prefer hybrid bikes. They're good on both roads and tracks, aren't they?
Agent: That's right. Hybrids for six. And where would you like to meet the guide? We can meet you at our shop in the town centre, or outside the railway station.
Caller: Most of us are coming by train, so the station would be easiest.
Agent: Outside the station, then.
Narrator: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.
Agent: Now, let me tell you about the three tours we run on Sundays. The first is the Coastal Trail. That's twenty-five kilometres, mostly flat, and the highlight is a visit to an old lighthouse, where you can climb to the top for the view. That one costs forty-five pounds per person.
Caller: Sounds good.
Agent: The second is the Forest Loop. It's shorter, at eighteen kilometres, but there are some steep sections. Halfway round there's a picnic lunch next to a waterfall, which people love, especially in summer. That's forty pounds each.
Caller: And the third?
Agent: The third is the Valley Route. It's the longest, at thirty kilometres, and it includes a stop at a cheese farm, where you can taste their products and see how they're made. The price for that one is fifty-five pounds, which includes the tasting and lunch.
Caller: Right. I'll talk to the others and call you back to confirm which one we choose.
Agent: No problem. I'll hold the date for you until Friday.
Narrator: That is the end of Part 1.

But once work started, engineers discovered that the foundations were unstable, and that's what turned a six-month project into a three-year one. The good news is that the museum has used the time to completely rethink how its collections are displayed.
Presenter: Entry to the permanent galleries remains free, as it always has been. However, there will be a charge of eight pounds for the special exhibitions, which will change every four months. Local residents can apply for an annual pass, which gives unlimited entry to all exhibitions for twenty pounds a year.
Presenter: Opening hours have changed, too. The museum used to close at five every day, but it will now stay open until nine on Thursday evenings, with talks and live music. It will, however, be closed on Mondays, which is when the staff carry out cleaning and maintenance.
Presenter: The museum's director told me that the main aim of the redesign was to attract more young people. Surveys showed that teenagers in particular found the old museum dull, so many of the new displays are interactive, and a group of local secondary school students helped to design the new natural history gallery.

Leah: That's right. What struck you most about it?
Sam: Honestly, I expected the story to be about their coffee, but it's really about location. They always opened next to universities and hospitals, places where people need coffee at all hours.
Leah: I agree. Their coffee isn't actually rated that highly. The prices are about average too.
Sam: So for our presentation, should we focus on the location strategy?
Leah: I think that should be the main part, yes. But we also need to say why they ran into trouble in the last two years.
Sam: That's the interesting bit. They expanded into shopping centres, which had nothing in common with their usual locations, and most of those branches lost money.
Leah: And at the same time online shopping was emptying the shopping centres. Bad timing.
Sam: What did you think of the way they dealt with it?
Leah: I thought it was impressive. Instead of cutting staff, which is what most companies do, they closed the shopping centre branches and moved the staff to new branches near train stations.
Sam: That's true. Although the case study doesn't really give us figures to show whether that worked.
Leah: No, which is a weakness. We should mention that.

listening.script:
Narrator: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about coral reef restoration. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
Lecturer: Good morning. In today's lecture I'll be looking at coral reefs, why they matter, what threatens them, and the methods scientists are using to restore them.
Lecturer: Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they support around a quarter of all marine species. They also protect coastlines. A healthy reef absorbs most of the energy of incoming waves, which reduces erosion and protects coastal communities from storms. And they're economically important: millions of people depend on reefs for fishing and tourism.
Lecturer: The greatest threat to reefs is rising sea temperature. Corals get most of their food from tiny algae that live inside their tissues. When the water becomes too warm, the corals expel these algae, and because the algae give coral its colour, the coral turns white. This is known as bleaching. A bleached coral isn't dead, but if high temperatures continue for several weeks, it will starve.
Lecturer: Other threats include pollution, especially fertiliser washed off farmland, which encourages the growth of seaweed that smothers the coral, and overfishing, which removes the fish that would normally graze on that seaweed.
Lecturer: So what can be done? The most widely used restoration technique is coral gardening. Small fragments of coral are grown in underwater nurseries, often hanging from structures that look rather like trees made of plastic pipe. When the fragments are large enough, divers attach them to damaged parts of the reef. It works, but it's slow and labour-intensive, and it can only cover small areas.
Lecturer: A faster approach is called micro-fragmenting. Researchers discovered, partly by accident, that when coral is cut into tiny pieces of just one or two square centimetres, each piece grows up to forty times faster than normal. Several pieces placed close together will eventually fuse into a single colony.
Lecturer: Another method uses sound. Healthy reefs are noisy places, full of the clicks and grunts of fish and shrimp. Degraded reefs are almost silent. In experiments in Australia, scientists placed underwater loudspeakers on dead patches of reef and played recordings of healthy reefs. The number of young fish arriving at these patches doubled, and those fish then helped to clean the reef.
Lecturer: Finally, some scientists are breeding corals that can tolerate heat. By selecting corals that survived bleaching events and breeding them together, they hope to produce populations that can cope with warmer seas. This is promising, but critics warn that it treats the symptoms rather than the cause.
Lecturer: Which brings me to my last point. None of these techniques will save reefs unless greenhouse gas emissions are reduced. Restoration buys time, but it can't keep pace with warming on its own.
Narrator: That is the end of Part 4.

reading.passage:
When a honeybee discovers a rich source of nectar, she does something remarkable on her return to the hive: she dances. For centuries, beekeepers had noticed bees moving in strange patterns on the honeycomb, but it was not until the 1940s that the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch showed that these movements carry precise information about where food can be found. His discovery, which earned him a share of the Nobel Prize in 1973, revealed one of the most sophisticated systems of communication known in any animal other than humans.

Von Frisch identified two main types of dance. When food is close to the hive, generally within about 50 metres, a returning forager performs a round dance, running in small circles, first one way and then the other. This tells her sisters that food is nearby, but not in which direction; they simply leave the hive and search the surrounding area, guided partly by the scent of the flowers that clings to the dancer's body. When food is further away, the bee performs the far more informative waggle dance.

In the waggle dance, the bee runs forward in a straight line while vibrating her abdomen from side to side, then circles back to her starting point and repeats the run, alternating between a loop to the left and a loop to the right. The direction of the straight run indicates the direction of the food. Because the dance takes place in the darkness of the hive, on a vertical sheet of honeycomb, the bee cannot point directly at the target. Instead, she uses gravity as a reference: running straight up the comb means fly towards the sun, while running at an angle of, say, 40 degrees to the right of vertical means fly at 40 degrees to the right of the sun. The duration of the waggle run indicates distance. Roughly speaking, each second of waggling corresponds to about one kilometre of flight, although the exact relationship varies between colonies.

Von Frisch's conclusions were not universally accepted. In the 1960s, the American biologist Adrian Wenner argued that bees found food using smell alone, and that the dance was a by-product of excitement rather than a message. The debate continued for decades. It was finally settled in 2005, when researchers in the United Kingdom fitted bees with tiny radar transponders and tracked their flights. Bees that had watched a dance flew directly towards the area indicated, then switched to searching by smell once they arrived, confirming that both the dance and scent play a role.

The dance also involves an element of decision-making. A bee that has found an especially rich source dances longer and more vigorously, recruiting more followers, whereas a poor source receives only a brief dance or none at all. In this way, a colony of tens of thousands of bees can direct its workforce to the best flowers without any individual bee comparing the options. A similar process is used when a swarm searches for a new home: scout bees dance for the sites they have inspected, and the site that attracts the most enthusiastic dancing eventually wins.

Modern research has revealed further subtleties. Bees appear to take account of the movement of the sun during the day, adjusting the angle of the dance as time passes, even if they have been inside the hive for some time. Studies have also found that the dance is partly learned. Young bees that were raised without older bees to observe performed disorganised dances at first, although their accuracy improved with experience.

Today, scientists are using the waggle dance in an unexpected way. By filming dances in hives and decoding them, researchers can map where a colony's bees are feeding across an entire landscape. This has allowed them to identify which habitats are most valuable to bees, and the results have been used to advise farmers and planners on where wildflowers should be planted. Von Frisch could hardly have imagined that his discovery would one day help to protect the insects he spent his life studying.

reading.passageTitle: Turning the Sea into Drinking Water
reading.passage:
A  Although water covers more than 70 per cent of the Earth's surface, less than one per cent of it is fresh water that is readily available for human use. As populations grow and droughts become more frequent, more and more countries are turning to the vast reserve that lies on their doorstep: the sea. Desalination, the removal of salt from seawater, is now carried out in more than 20,000 plants worldwide, supplying drinking water to around 300 million people. In some countries in the Middle East, it provides the majority of the domestic water supply.

B  The oldest method is distillation, which imitates the natural water cycle. Seawater is heated until it evaporates, leaving the salt behind, and the steam is then cooled and collected as fresh water. Sailors used simple versions of this technique as early as the fourth century BC. Large distillation plants were built in the Gulf states from the 1960s onwards, where cheap oil and gas made the enormous energy requirements affordable. Many of these plants are combined with power stations, using the waste heat from electricity generation.

C  Since the 1980s, however, distillation has been largely overtaken by reverse osmosis. In this process, seawater is forced at very high pressure through membranes with pores so small that water molecules can pass through, but salt and most other impurities cannot. Reverse osmosis uses far less energy than distillation, typically between a third and a half as much, because the water does not need to be boiled. Improvements in membranes and in devices that recover energy from the high-pressure waste stream have cut its energy use by more than 75 per cent since 1980.

D  Even so, desalination remains expensive. Producing a cubic metre of drinking water from the sea typically costs several times more than treating water from a river or an underground aquifer. Energy accounts for up to half of the operating cost, which means the price of desalinated water rises and falls with the price of electricity. Building a large plant can cost more than a billion dollars, and it may take years to win approval. For these reasons, desalination is usually seen as a last resort, to be used when cheaper sources have been exhausted.

E  There are also environmental concerns. For every litre of fresh water produced, a typical plant releases about one and a half litres of brine, a highly concentrated salt solution that often also contains chemicals used to clean the membranes. Because brine is denser than seawater, it sinks and can form a layer on the seabed, reducing oxygen levels and harming marine life. The intake pipes that draw in seawater can also trap fish and other organisms. Engineers are trying to reduce these impacts by spreading the brine through diffusers, which mix it rapidly with the surrounding water, and by placing intakes beneath the sea floor.

F  Researchers are exploring several ways to make desalination cheaper and cleaner. Some plants are now powered entirely by solar or wind energy, which reduces their carbon emissions and protects them from fluctuating fuel prices. Others are experimenting with extracting valuable materials from brine, such as magnesium and lithium, which could turn a waste product into a source of income. Meanwhile, new membranes made from materials such as graphene could, in theory, let water through far more easily, reducing the pressure, and therefore the energy, required. Whether these technologies can be scaled up remains to be seen, but for many dry regions of the world, the sea may become an increasingly important source of water.

reading.passage:
Of the roughly 7,000 languages spoken in the world today, linguists estimate that around half may disappear by the end of this century. Many are already spoken only by a handful of elderly people; when the last of them dies, the language will vanish, often without ever having been written down. The loss is rarely sudden. More often, a language dies over several generations, as parents decide that their children's futures lie in a more widely spoken language and stop passing on their own.

The reasons are usually economic and social rather than the result of deliberate suppression, although suppression has certainly played its part. In the past, many governments punished children for speaking minority languages at school. Today the pressure is subtler. Jobs, education and the media are dominated by national and global languages, and young people understandably want access to them. Migration to cities accelerates the process, because families from different language communities mix and adopt a common language. The linguist Nicholas Ostler has observed that languages rarely die because people are forced to abandon them; they die because people stop believing that their language is useful.

Why should the disappearance of a language matter? One answer is scientific. Each language represents a unique solution to the problem of human communication, and linguists can only understand the full range of what human languages can do by studying as many as possible. Some languages have features that were once thought impossible. Pirahã, spoken in the Brazilian Amazon, has been claimed to lack words for exact numbers, a claim that, if true, challenges basic assumptions about human cognition, although other researchers dispute it.

A second argument concerns knowledge. Languages often contain detailed information about the local environment, built up over centuries. Indigenous languages in many regions have names for hundreds of plants and animals, along with knowledge of their uses, much of which has never been recorded by science. The ethnobotanist David Harrison has argued that when a language dies, we lose not just words but an entire library of ecological knowledge. Critics reply that such knowledge can be translated and preserved in other languages, but Harrison maintains that much of it is embedded in the structure of the language itself and is lost in translation.

The third argument is about identity and rights. For many communities, their language is inseparable from their culture, history and sense of who they are. Studies of indigenous communities in Canada found that youth suicide rates were dramatically lower in communities where a majority of people could speak the traditional language. The researchers were careful to say that this does not prove that language itself protects young people, since language knowledge may simply reflect other factors, such as strong community institutions. Nevertheless, the finding has been influential.

Can dying languages be revived? The most famous success is Hebrew, which for centuries was used mainly for religious and written purposes and was revived as an everyday spoken language in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries. It now has millions of native speakers. Welsh, too, has stabilised after a long decline, helped by Welsh-medium schools and a Welsh-language television channel. In New Zealand, the Māori community set up language nests, preschools in which young children are surrounded by fluent elderly speakers, and the model has since been copied around the world.

Yet these successes share conditions that many endangered languages lack: a substantial number of speakers, political support and, crucially, a community determined to use the language in daily life. Technology can help. Smartphone apps, online dictionaries and social media allow scattered speakers to communicate and learners to study. But recording a language is not the same as keeping it alive. A language preserved in an archive is like a pressed flower, beautiful perhaps, but no longer growing. In my view, the most valuable thing outsiders can do is not to document endangered languages, important as that is, but to support the communities who want to keep speaking them.

The diagram below shows the process by which glass bottles are recycled.

Stage 1: Used bottles are collected from bottle banks and household recycling bins.
Stage 2: The bottles are taken by lorry to a recycling plant.
Stage 3: They are sorted by colour (clear, green and brown).
Stage 4: Labels, lids and other contaminants are removed.

Stage 6: The cullet is mixed with sand, soda ash and limestone.

Stage 8: The molten glass is shaped into new bottles.
Stage 9: The new bottles are filled and delivered to shops.

listening.script:
Narrator: Part 1. You will hear a student talking to an accommodation officer about staying with a host family. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.
Officer: Hello, come in. You're here about homestay accommodation?
Student: Yes, that's right. I'm starting an English course here next month and I'd like to live with a local family.
Officer: Lovely. I'll just fill in the application form with you. What's your full name?
Student: Daniel Okafor. The surname is O, K, A, F, O, R.
Officer: Thank you. And how old are you, Daniel?
Student: I'm twenty-three. I'll be twenty-four in December.
Officer: So twenty-three for now. Which course are you taking?
Student: It's the business English course, the evening one, because I'll be doing an internship during the day.
Officer: Right, business English. And how long would you like to stay with a family?
Student: The course lasts twelve weeks, but I'm planning to travel for the last two, so ten weeks, please.
Officer: Ten weeks. Do you have any dietary requirements?
Student: I don't eat meat, but I do eat fish. So I suppose I'm not completely vegetarian.
Officer: That's fine, I'll write no meat. Families are usually happy to cook fish. Do you have any allergies?
Student: Only to cats. Dogs are fine, but cats make me sneeze terribly.
Officer: OK, so no cats in the house.
Narrator: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.
Officer: Now, let me tell you about a couple of families who might suit you. The first is the Harris family. They live in Westfield, which is about twenty-five minutes from the college by bus. There's a couple in their fifties, and their son, who's at university, so he'd be someone your age to talk to.
Student: That sounds nice.
Officer: The only thing is that they ask guests to be home by eleven on weekdays, because they get up early.
Student: Hmm, my class finishes at nine, so that should be fine.
Officer: The second family is the Lins, in Parkside. That's closer, only a ten-minute walk, but it's a busier household. They have three young children, so it can be noisy.
Student: I think I'd find it hard to study with three young children around.
Officer: That's understandable. So shall I put you forward for the Harris family?
Student: Yes, please.
Officer: Great. The weekly charge is one hundred and sixty pounds, and that includes breakfast and an evening meal every day. On weekdays you'll be out at lunchtime anyway. The first payment is due one week before you arrive, and you can pay by bank transfer.
Student: That's fine. And will I meet them before I move in?
Officer: We usually arrange a video call first, so you can introduce yourselves. I'll email you to set it up.
Narrator: That is the end of Part 1.

listening.scriptTitle: New services at the city library
listening.script:
Narrator: Part 2. You will hear a librarian talking to a group of visitors about changes at the city library. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
Librarian: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming to this open evening. As many of you know, the library has just completed a major refurbishment, and I'd like to tell you about some of the changes and new services.
Librarian: Let's start with membership. Joining the library has always been free for people who live in the city, and that hasn't changed. What's new is that people who work in the city but live elsewhere can now join free of charge as well. Previously they had to pay an annual fee. You'll still need to bring some identification, but we no longer ask for proof of address if you join online.
Librarian: We've also changed the rules on borrowing. Members can now borrow up to fifteen items at a time, rather than ten. And you'll be pleased to hear that we've abolished fines for late returns altogether. Research from other libraries showed that fines discouraged people, especially families, from using the library at all, and very few items are lost as a result.
Librarian: One of the most popular new features is the self-service machines by the entrance. You can borrow and return items there, and also pay for printing. Staff are still available at the information desk, of course, and they now have much more time to help people with research and with using computers.
Librarian: On that subject, we're offering free digital skills sessions every Tuesday morning. These were originally intended for older people, but in fact many of those attending have been job seekers who want help writing their applications online, so we're adding an extra session on Friday afternoons aimed specifically at them.
Narrator: Now look at questions 16 to 20.
Librarian: Let me now tell you what you'll find in each part of the building. The ground floor is where most visitors start. It's where you'll find newspapers and magazines, and the self-service machines I mentioned. We've also moved the children's library to the ground floor, so that families with pushchairs don't need to use the lift.
Librarian: The first floor is home to adult fiction and non-fiction. It also has our brand new music room, which is soundproofed. You can book it for an hour at a time to practise an instrument. There's a piano in there, too.
Librarian: The second floor is the quiet floor. It contains the reference collection and individual study desks, and the local history archive, where you can look at old maps and photographs of the city. Phone calls aren't allowed anywhere on that floor.
Librarian: And finally, the top floor. This used to be offices, but it's been turned into what we call the makerspace. It has 3D printers, a laser cutter and sewing machines, and anyone over sixteen can use them after a short training session. There's also a small roof garden up there, which is maintained by volunteers and is a lovely place to read on a sunny day.
Narrator: That is the end of Part 2.

listening.scriptTitle: An experiment on music and memory
listening.script:
Narrator: Part 3. You will hear two psychology students, Ryan and Priya, discussing their experiment with their tutor. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.
Tutor: So, Ryan, Priya, tell me how the experiment on music and memory went.
Ryan: Well, we tested forty participants. Half of them memorised a list of words in silence, and the other half while listening to music.
Tutor: And how did you choose the music?
Priya: At first we were going to let people choose their own favourite songs, but we realised that would make it impossible to compare the groups. So in the end everyone in the music group heard the same piece, a piano recording without any words.
Tutor: Good. Lyrics would definitely have interfered with remembering words. Where did you find your participants?
Ryan: We'd planned to recruit students from the library, but most people said they were too busy. In the end we put a notice on the psychology department's website and got volunteers that way.
Tutor: That might be a limitation, because psychology students may guess what you're testing.
Priya: Yes, we've noted that.
Tutor: And the results?
Ryan: The silent group remembered more words on average, which is what most previous studies found. But what we didn't expect was that the difference disappeared for people who said they usually study with music.
Tutor: That's very interesting. It suggests that habit matters. Did you ask people how often they study with music?
Priya: Only as a yes or no question. Looking back, we should have used a scale, from never to always.
Tutor: That would certainly have given you more useful data. What will you do with the report now?
Ryan: We were thinking of presenting it at the student research conference in May.
Tutor: I'd encourage that. But before you do, I'd run the experiment again with a larger sample. Forty is quite small.
Narrator: Now look at questions 26 to 30.
Tutor: Let's think about how you'll present each part of the report. How are you going to show the main results?
Priya: We were going to use a table, but I think a bar chart would make the difference between the groups clearer.
Tutor: I agree. And the background?
Ryan: We've written a lot about the history of research into music and memory, going back to the nineteen-nineties.
Tutor: Keep that brief. Focus on the two or three studies most similar to yours.
Priya: For the procedure, we've described it in a long paragraph.
Tutor: It would be easier to follow as a numbered list of steps.
Ryan: And the participant information? We have the age and gender of everyone.
Tutor: That doesn't need to be in the main report at all. Put it in an appendix.
Priya: And the discussion?
Tutor: That's the most important part. Make sure you discuss the unexpected finding about habit in detail. That's what will make your report stand out.
Narrator: That is the end of Part 3.

listening.script:
Narrator: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the history of timekeeping. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
Lecturer: Today we're going to look at how humans have measured time, and how changes in timekeeping have shaped society.
Lecturer: The earliest timekeeping devices relied on the sun. The ancient Egyptians used tall stone columns called obelisks, whose shadows moved across the ground as the day went on. Later, they developed portable sundials. The obvious weakness of any sundial is that it's useless at night and on cloudy days.
Lecturer: To solve this, people turned to water. The water clock, which the Greeks called a clepsydra, measured time by the steady flow of water out of a container. Water clocks were used in Athenian courts to limit the length of speeches, so that each speaker had the same amount of time. Their main drawback was that the flow changed with temperature, because water flows more slowly when it is cold.
Lecturer: Mechanical clocks appeared in Europe in the late thirteenth century, mostly in the towers of churches and monasteries. Monks needed to know when to pray at fixed times through the day and night. These early clocks had no faces at all. Instead, they rang bells, and in fact the word clock comes from an old word meaning bell. They were also very inaccurate, gaining or losing as much as fifteen minutes a day.
Lecturer: The great breakthrough came in 1656, when the Dutch scientist Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock. A pendulum swings at a very regular rate, and Huygens's clock reduced the error to less than a minute a day. For the first time it became worthwhile to add a minute hand.
Lecturer: However, pendulum clocks didn't work at sea, because the motion of the ship disturbed the pendulum. This was a serious problem, because sailors needed accurate time to calculate their longitude, their position east or west. In 1714 the British government offered a huge prize for a solution, and it was eventually won by a carpenter, John Harrison, whose marine chronometer lost only a few seconds over a long voyage.
Lecturer: Now, here's something that surprises many students. Until the nineteenth century, every town set its clocks by its own local noon, when the sun was highest. So the time in Bristol was about ten minutes behind London. It was the railways that changed this. Timetables were impossible to manage with dozens of local times, so in 1847 British railway companies adopted a single standard time. Within a few decades, standard time zones had been agreed across much of the world.
Lecturer: In the twentieth century, accuracy improved even further, first with quartz clocks, which use the vibrations of a crystal, and then with atomic clocks, which measure the vibrations of atoms. The best atomic clocks today would lose less than a second in hundreds of millions of years, and they're essential to satellite navigation systems on your phone.
Narrator: That is the end of Part 4.

reading.passage:
In 2007, eleven countries along the southern edge of the Sahara Desert launched one of the most ambitious environmental projects ever attempted. The plan was to plant a continuous belt of trees, some 15 kilometres wide and nearly 8,000 kilometres long, stretching across Africa from Senegal in the west to Djibouti in the east. This Great Green Wall, as it became known, was intended to halt the advance of the desert into the Sahel, the semi-arid region that lies between the Sahara and the wetter savannahs further south.

The problem it set out to address is real. The Sahel is home to more than 100 million people, most of whom depend on farming and herding. Over recent decades, a combination of droughts, population growth, overgrazing and the clearing of trees for fuel has left large areas of land degraded, with soils too poor to grow crops. When the vegetation disappears, wind and rain strip away the fertile topsoil, and the land becomes increasingly difficult to restore. The resulting poverty has driven many young people to migrate, either to cities or abroad.

The early years of the project, however, were disappointing. Planting trees in a dry region turned out to be far harder than planting them on a map. Seedlings were often raised in distant nurseries and planted by people who had little interest in their survival. In some areas, as many as 80 per cent of the trees planted died within a few years, because they were not watered, were eaten by livestock, or were species unsuited to local conditions. By 2020, only around four per cent of the original target had been reached, and critics described the wall as a costly illusion.

Yet even as the original vision faltered, a different approach was proving its worth. In southern Niger, farmers had discovered in the 1980s that their fields contained a hidden forest: a network of living tree roots and stumps that survived beneath the surface even after the trees themselves had been cut down. By selecting the strongest shoots growing from these stumps, protecting them and pruning them carefully, farmers could regrow trees at almost no cost. This technique, known as farmer-managed natural regeneration, has since spread across more than five million hectares in Niger alone.

The benefits have been considerable. Trees growing among crops reduce wind speed, protect the soil and add nutrients to it as their leaves fall. Many species provide fruit, animal fodder and medicines, and the wood from pruned branches can be used or sold as fuel. Studies have found that crop yields in fields with trees can be significantly higher than in fields without them, and that households practising regeneration are better able to cope with drought.

As a result, the Great Green Wall has been redefined. Rather than a single line of trees, it is now described as a mosaic of different land-use practices, including natural regeneration, water harvesting and the protection of grazing land, carried out by local communities across the whole Sahel. Techniques such as zaï pits, small holes dug in hard ground and filled with compost to capture rainwater, have allowed farmers in Burkina Faso to grow crops on land that had been abandoned for years.

The redefined project has attracted large international commitments, including pledges of more than 14 billion dollars in 2021. But money alone will not guarantee success. Researchers emphasise that the most important factor is whether local people have secure rights to the land and the trees on it. Where farmers fear that trees they have nurtured will be taken by others, or that they will need official permission to use them, they have little reason to invest their time. Where those rights are clear, the evidence suggests that the Sahel can become green again, not through a wall, but through millions of individual decisions.

reading.passageTitle: Learning Through Play: The Rise of Gamification
reading.passage:
A  Gamification, the use of elements from games in non-game settings, has spread rapidly through education over the past fifteen years. Points, badges, leaderboards and levels now feature in language-learning apps, school maths platforms and university courses. The appeal is easy to understand. Games are extraordinarily good at holding attention: millions of people voluntarily spend hours mastering difficult video games, while many students struggle to stay focused on homework for twenty minutes. If even a fraction of that motivation could be transferred to learning, the benefits would be enormous.

B  The idea is not entirely new. Teachers have long used gold stars, house points and classroom quizzes to encourage effort. What is different today is the scale and precision made possible by digital technology. An app can track every answer a learner gives, reward them instantly, adjust the difficulty of the next task and compare their progress with that of thousands of others. Streaks, which count the number of consecutive days a learner has practised, have proved especially powerful in keeping people coming back.

C  Research on the effectiveness of gamification is mixed, however. A number of reviews have concluded that, on average, gamified learning produces modest improvements in engagement and slightly smaller improvements in actual learning. But the average hides wide variation. Some studies report large gains; others find no effect, and a few find that gamified courses performed worse than conventional ones. Much depends on which elements are used and how.

D  One concern is the effect of rewards on motivation. Psychologists distinguish between intrinsic motivation, doing something because it is interesting or satisfying in itself, and extrinsic motivation, doing it to gain a reward or avoid a punishment. A substantial body of research suggests that offering rewards for an activity people already enjoy can reduce their intrinsic interest in it, a phenomenon known as the overjustification effect. In a classic experiment, children who were promised a certificate for drawing later spent less time drawing freely than children who had not been offered one. Critics fear that badges and points may teach learners to value the reward rather than the knowledge.

E  Leaderboards raise particular problems. For learners near the top, public rankings can be highly motivating. For those near the bottom, they can be discouraging and even humiliating, leading some to give up altogether. Some designers have responded by showing learners only how they compare with others of a similar level, or by replacing rankings with personal goals, so that progress is measured against one's own past performance rather than against classmates.

F  The most successful examples of gamification tend to borrow more than the surface features of games. Good games give players clear goals, immediate feedback, challenges that increase gradually in difficulty and the freedom to fail without serious consequences. These principles are well supported by research on learning. A student who can attempt a problem, see instantly what went wrong and try again is likely to learn more than one who waits a week for a marked assignment. Seen in this light, the value of gamification may lie less in points and badges than in the way it encourages better teaching design.

G  Perhaps the clearest lesson from the research is that gamification is a tool, not a solution. Used thoughtfully, it can make practice more engaging and help learners build regular habits. Used carelessly, it can turn learning into a hunt for points. As one researcher has put it, the question is not whether to gamify, but what exactly we want learners to be motivated to do.

reading.passage:
In medicine, a placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient: a sugar pill, an injection of salt water, or even a sham operation in which the surgeon makes an incision but performs no procedure. For centuries, placebos were regarded as little more than a trick, useful for satisfying patients who demanded treatment when none was available. Since the 1950s, however, they have played a central role in medical research. In a controlled trial, one group of patients receives the new drug and another receives a placebo that looks identical. Only if the drug performs significantly better than the placebo is it considered effective.

The reason for this design is that patients who receive placebos often improve, sometimes dramatically. In trials of treatments for pain, depression and irritable bowel syndrome, a substantial proportion of patients in the placebo group report real relief. For a long time, this was explained away. Some patients would have recovered anyway, since many conditions get better on their own; others might simply be telling researchers what they thought they wanted to hear. These factors certainly play a part. But over the past few decades, scientists have shown that placebo responses can also involve measurable changes in the body.

Some of the clearest evidence comes from studies of pain. In the 1970s, researchers found that the pain relief produced by a placebo could be blocked by naloxone, a drug that prevents the action of the body's natural painkillers, known as endorphins. This suggested that the expectation of relief was triggering the release of endorphins. Brain-imaging studies have since shown that placebos can reduce activity in areas of the brain that process pain. In patients with Parkinson's disease, placebos have been found to increase the release of dopamine, the chemical messenger whose shortage causes the disease's symptoms.

Expectation is not the only mechanism. Conditioning, a form of learning, also plays a role. If a patient repeatedly takes a drug that suppresses the immune system, and then later takes an identical-looking pill without the drug, the immune system may respond as though the drug were present. The body, in effect, learns to associate the pill with its effect. This has led some researchers to propose that doses of certain drugs could be reduced by alternating real pills with placebos, lowering side effects and costs.

The context in which treatment is given also matters a great deal. Studies have found that two placebo pills work better than one, that injections tend to work better than pills, and that branded placebos work better than unbranded ones. Even the colour of a pill makes a difference: in some studies, blue placebos were more effective as sleeping pills, while red ones worked better as stimulants. Perhaps most significantly, the warmth and attention of the person providing treatment can strengthen the response. In one study of irritable bowel syndrome, patients who received placebo treatment from a friendly, attentive practitioner improved considerably more than those treated by a practitioner who was brief and formal.

Using placebos in ordinary medical practice, however, raises a difficult ethical question. If a doctor tells a patient that a pill contains an active drug when it does not, the doctor is deceiving the patient, and trust between doctors and patients depends on honesty. A surprising finding may offer a way out. In several studies, patients were given placebos and told openly that the pills contained no medicine, but that placebos had been shown to help many people. Even so, many of them improved. These open-label placebos appear to work best for conditions with subjective symptoms, such as pain and fatigue, and the reasons are not yet fully understood.

It would be a mistake, though, to overstate what placebos can do. They can ease the symptoms a patient experiences, but there is little evidence that they can shrink tumours, kill infections or repair damaged tissue. A patient with asthma who takes a placebo inhaler may feel less breathless, yet tests show that the airways remain as narrow as before. In my view, the real lesson of placebo research is not that patients should be given sugar pills, but that the way care is delivered, with time, attention and clear explanation, is itself a powerful part of treatment, one that modern medicine, with its short appointments, too often neglects.

listening.script:
Narrator: Part 1. You will hear a woman reporting a lost bag at a railway lost property office. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.
Clerk: Good morning, lost property. How can I help?
Woman: Hello. I left a bag on a train yesterday evening, and I'm hoping someone has handed it in.
Clerk: I'll take the details and check our system. Which train were you on?
Woman: The six forty-five from Manchester to Leeds. I got off at Leeds and only realised about an hour later.
Clerk: Six forty-five, Manchester to Leeds. Can you describe the bag?
Woman: It's a small backpack, dark green, with a brown leather strap on the front.
Clerk: Dark green backpack. Any brand name?
Woman: Yes, it's made by a company called Halvern. H, A, L, V, E, R, N.
Clerk: And what was inside?
Woman: The most important thing is my laptop. There was also a scarf, and a book I'd borrowed from the library, which I really need to return.
Clerk: Was there anything with your name on it?
Woman: The library book has a library card inside it, as a bookmark actually. So that would have my name.
Clerk: That's helpful. And where in the train did you leave it? On the luggage rack?
Woman: No, I put it on the floor, under my seat. I think I was in the second carriage from the front.
Clerk: OK. Now I need your contact details. What's your name?
Woman: Rebecca Stanton.
Clerk: And a phone number?
Woman: It's oh seven nine four six, two two one, five eight three.
Narrator: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.
Clerk: Right, I've checked the system, and I'm afraid nothing matching that description has been handed in yet. But items from yesterday evening's trains often don't reach us until the following afternoon, because they're collected by the cleaning teams overnight.
Woman: Oh, I see.
Clerk: If it does come in, we'll send you a text message. We don't ring people any more because so many calls were missed.
Woman: And would I have to collect it from here?
Clerk: You can collect it here, or we can send it to any staffed station on the network for a small fee. Collecting it here is free.
Woman: I'll come here. I work nearby. What will I need to bring?
Clerk: Photo identification, such as a passport or driving licence. And since there's a laptop involved, we'll ask you to tell us the password, or show that it opens with your fingerprint, just to prove it's yours.
Woman: That's fine. How long do you keep things?
Clerk: We keep items for three months. After that, anything valuable is sold at auction and the money goes to charity.
Woman: Let's hope it doesn't come to that! Thank you very much.
Narrator: That is the end of Part 1.

Narrator: Part 2. You will hear the manager of an outdoor activity centre talking to parents about a summer camp. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
Manager: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. I'm Laura, the manager here at Pinewood Outdoor Centre, and I'd like to explain how the summer camp works before your children join us next month.
Manager: First of all, groups. Children are placed in groups of eight, each with its own instructor. We used to group children by age, but we found that friendships matter far more to how much children enjoy the week, so now we ask each child to name two friends, and we make sure they're in a group with at least one of them.
Manager: As for safety, all our instructors hold first aid qualifications, and there's a nurse on site twenty-four hours a day. The question parents ask most often is about the lake. Children only go on the water with an instructor, and everyone wears a life jacket, even strong swimmers.
Manager: Now, phones. Many parents are surprised to hear that we ask children to hand in their phones on arrival. We tried allowing them for a year, and we found that children who spent the evenings on their phones were more likely to feel homesick, not less. Instead, we post photos on a private website every evening, so you can see what they've been doing.
Manager: Food is cooked fresh on site, and we can cater for all dietary needs, as long as you tell us at least two weeks before the camp starts. Please don't send children with sweets or snacks, as we have problems with mice in the cabins.
Manager: And finally, what to pack. You'll find a list on our website, but the one thing children most often forget is a torch. The paths between the cabins aren't lit at night, so they really do need one.
Narrator: Now look at questions 16 to 20.
Manager: Let me run through the week. On Monday, after the children arrive and settle in, they'll do a series of team games, which are designed to help the groups get to know each other.
Manager: Tuesday is the day most children look forward to, because it's the day of the high ropes course, where they climb and balance on ropes and platforms high in the trees.
Manager: On Wednesday, the groups go out to the lake for canoeing. If the weather's too windy, we swap Wednesday and Thursday around.
Manager: Thursday is spent in the forest, where children learn bushcraft skills, such as building shelters and lighting a fire safely, and in the evening they cook their own dinner on the fire they've made.
Manager: Friday morning is a treasure hunt, using maps and compasses, which gives them a chance to use the navigation skills they've learned during the week. And on Friday afternoon, parents are invited to a short show, where each group performs a sketch about their week, before you take them home.
Narrator: That is the end of Part 2.

listening.scriptTitle: A report on a factory visit
listening.script:
Narrator: Part 3. You will hear two engineering students, Olivia and Tom, talking to their tutor about a visit to a bicycle factory. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.
Tutor: So, how was the visit to the factory?
Olivia: Really useful. I'd never seen a production line in real life before.
Tutor: What impressed you most?
Tom: I thought it would be the robots, but actually it was how much of the work is still done by hand. The wheels, for example, are built by people, because the factory manager said machines can't yet tension the spokes accurately enough.
Olivia: For me it was the testing. Every frame is tested to destruction, well, one in every hundred is. They put it in a machine that bends it thousands of times until it breaks.
Tutor: Did you get a chance to talk to the engineers?
Tom: Yes, one of the design engineers spent nearly an hour with us. She said the biggest challenge in her job isn't the technology, it's that customers want bikes to be lighter and cheaper at the same time.
Olivia: She also said the factory moved production back from Asia three years ago. Mainly so they could respond faster when designs change, rather than because of cost.
Tutor: Interesting. Now, your report. Have you decided on a focus?
Tom: We were going to write about the whole factory, but there's too much. So we're going to focus on quality control.
Tutor: Good, that's manageable. And have you thought about what you'll compare it with?
Olivia: We could compare it with the car factory we visited last year.
Tutor: That would work well, since you've got notes from that visit too.
Narrator: Now look at questions 26 to 30.
Tutor: Let's think about what each of you will do. Who's going to write up the interview with the engineer?
Tom: I recorded it, so I'll do that.
Tutor: And the photographs?
Olivia: I took most of them, so I'll choose which ones to use and write the captions.
Tutor: What about the background research on the company's history?
Tom: Neither of us has started that. Shall we share it?
Olivia: Yes, let's do half each.
Tutor: And the data from the testing machine? You said they gave you a spreadsheet.
Olivia: That's more my thing. I'll analyse it and make the graphs.
Tutor: And the comparison with the car factory?
Tom: I'll do that, because I was the one who wrote the report on the car factory last year.
Tutor: Sounds like a sensible plan.
Narrator: That is the end of Part 3.
