listening.script:
Narrator: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about animal navigation. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
Lecturer: Good morning. Today's topic is one of the great puzzles of biology: how animals find their way across enormous distances, often to places they have never been before.
Lecturer: Let's begin with birds. The Arctic tern, for example, flies from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back every year, a round trip of around seventy thousand kilometres. Birds use several sources of information. During the day, many use the position of the sun. But because the sun moves across the sky, they need an internal clock to compensate for the time of day. If you shift a pigeon's body clock by keeping it under artificial light, it will fly off in the wrong direction by a predictable amount.
Lecturer: At night, migrating birds use the stars. Experiments in planetariums in the nineteen sixties showed that young birds learn to recognise the point around which the night sky rotates, which in the northern hemisphere is close to the Pole Star.
Lecturer: Birds can also detect the Earth's magnetic field. This was once considered impossible, but it is now well established. The most widely accepted explanation involves a protein in the bird's eye, which may allow it to actually see the magnetic field as a pattern of light and shade.
Lecturer: Sea turtles provide another fascinating example. Female loggerhead turtles return to lay their eggs on the same beach where they themselves hatched, sometimes decades earlier. Research suggests that each stretch of coastline has its own magnetic signature, and that young turtles imprint on this signature when they first enter the sea.
Lecturer: Salmon, too, return to the river where they were born, but they use a different sense for the final part of the journey. Once they reach the coast, they follow the smell of their home river, which is unique because of the particular mixture of soil and plants in its area.
Lecturer: Even insects navigate in sophisticated ways. Monarch butterflies in North America travel up to four thousand kilometres to spend the winter in a small area of forest in Mexico. Remarkably, no individual butterfly makes the round trip. The journey north takes several generations, so the butterflies that fly south have never been there before.
Lecturer: Finally, a word about the threats these animals face. Artificial light at night can confuse migrating birds, causing them to collide with buildings. Some cities now ask office buildings to switch off their lights during peak migration seasons. And there is growing concern that human-made electromagnetic noise, from electrical equipment, may interfere with the magnetic sense of birds, although more research is needed before we can be sure.
Narrator: That is the end of Part 4.

reading.passage:
For most of human history, writing was done on materials that were either expensive, heavy or fragile. The Sumerians pressed marks into clay tablets; the Egyptians wrote on papyrus, made from strips of a reed that grew along the Nile; and in medieval Europe, important documents were written on parchment, prepared from the skins of animals. A single large book might require the skins of more than a hundred sheep. Paper, by comparison, could be made cheaply from almost any plant fibre, and its invention transformed the way knowledge was recorded and shared.

According to Chinese tradition, paper was invented in AD 105 by Cai Lun, an official at the imperial court, who made sheets from the bark of mulberry trees, old rags and fishing nets. Archaeologists have since found fragments of paper in China that are at least two centuries older, so it seems that Cai Lun improved and standardised an existing process rather than inventing it from nothing. Nevertheless, his methods were adopted throughout the empire, and paper quickly replaced bamboo strips and silk as the main material for writing in China.

The basic process has changed surprisingly little. Plant fibres are soaked and beaten until they separate into a pulp, which is mixed with water. A fine screen is dipped into the mixture and lifted out, leaving a thin layer of fibres on its surface. As the water drains away, the fibres bond together, and the resulting sheet is pressed and dried. The quality of paper depends largely on the length of the fibres and how thoroughly they have been beaten.

For several centuries, the technique remained a closely guarded secret. It spread first to Korea and Japan, and then, according to a well-known account, westward after the Battle of Talas in 751, when Arab forces captured Chinese soldiers who knew how to make paper. Historians now consider this story too simple, as paper was probably already known in Central Asia by then. What is certain is that by the end of the eighth century, paper was being produced in Baghdad, which became a major centre of learning. The availability of cheap paper contributed to a flourishing of scholarship, as scholars copied and translated works on mathematics, medicine and astronomy.

Paper reached Europe through the Islamic world, arriving in Spain in the eleventh century. At first, many Europeans regarded it with suspicion. In 1231, the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II declared that official documents written on paper were not legally valid, because parchment was considered more durable. Paper mills nevertheless spread steadily across Europe, often powered by water wheels that drove heavy hammers to beat rags into pulp.

The real turning point came with the printing press, developed by Johannes Gutenberg in the mid-fifteenth century. Printing on parchment was possible, but far too expensive for large numbers of copies. Paper made it economically possible to produce books in their thousands. Demand soon grew so fast that there were shortages of rags, and in some places governments even passed laws restricting the use of linen for burying the dead so that it could be used for paper instead.

The rag shortage was finally solved in the nineteenth century, when inventors developed methods of making paper from wood pulp. Wood was abundant and cheap, and newspapers, books and paper packaging became available to ordinary people on an unprecedented scale. The cost was paid in other ways: early wood-pulp paper contained acids that caused it to turn yellow and crumble within decades, which is why many nineteenth-century books are now in worse condition than books printed four hundred years earlier.

reading.passage:
A  The advice to sleep on a problem before making a decision is found in many languages, and for good reason. Over the past three decades, sleep researchers have accumulated strong evidence that sleep is not simply a period of rest, but an active state in which the brain processes and stores the information it has taken in during the day. People who sleep after learning a list of words, a sequence of movements or a new skill typically perform better when tested later than people who have spent the same amount of time awake.

B  To understand why, it helps to know that sleep is not uniform. Through the night, we cycle repeatedly through different stages, each cycle lasting around ninety minutes. Deep sleep, also called slow-wave sleep, is concentrated in the early part of the night, while rapid eye movement, or REM, sleep, during which most vivid dreaming occurs, dominates the hours before waking. Different stages appear to support different kinds of memory, which means that cutting sleep short at either end of the night may have different consequences.

C  Deep sleep seems especially important for memories of facts and events. During the day, new memories are stored temporarily in the hippocampus, a small structure deep in the brain. During deep sleep, the hippocampus appears to replay recent experiences, and these replays help transfer the memories to the cortex, the outer layer of the brain, for long-term storage. In experiments with rats that had learned to navigate a maze, researchers recorded the same patterns of brain activity during sleep that had occurred while the rats were running the maze, but at a much faster speed.

D  Remarkably, this process can be influenced from outside. In one study, participants learned the locations of objects on a screen while a particular sound or smell was present. When the same sound or smell was presented again while they were in deep sleep, they later remembered the locations better than those who had not been exposed to the cue. Such findings have raised the possibility of using cues to strengthen learning during sleep, though researchers stress that sleep cannot be used to learn entirely new material, such as a foreign language, from scratch.

E  REM sleep, by contrast, has been linked to emotional processing and to creativity. In a well-known experiment, participants were given a mathematical task that could be solved much faster using a hidden rule. Those who slept for a night between attempts were more than twice as likely to discover the rule as those who stayed awake. Some researchers believe that during REM sleep the brain makes unusual connections between memories, which may help explain why solutions sometimes appear to arrive overnight.

F  These findings have practical implications, particularly for students. Staying up all night to revise before an exam, a common habit, is likely to be counterproductive, because it deprives the brain of the sleep needed to consolidate what has been studied. A study of university students found that those who regularly slept at irregular times achieved lower grades than those with consistent sleep patterns, even when the total amount of sleep was similar. Many schools have also experimented with later start times for teenagers, whose body clocks naturally shift later during adolescence. Several studies report improvements in attendance and alertness, although the effect on exam results is less clear.

reading.passage:
In 1976, an economics professor in Bangladesh named Muhammad Yunus lent 27 dollars of his own money to a group of 42 women in a village near his university. The women made bamboo stools and had been borrowing from moneylenders at such high rates of interest that they kept almost nothing of what they earned. With Yunus's loan they were able to buy materials directly, sell their products at a fair price and repay him in full. From this small experiment grew the Grameen Bank, and with it a global movement known as microfinance: the provision of small loans to people too poor to borrow from conventional banks.

Conventional banks had long avoided lending to the very poor for understandable reasons. The amounts involved were tiny, so the cost of processing each loan was high relative to the interest it would earn. Poor borrowers rarely had property to offer as security, and banks had no way of judging whether they were likely to repay. Grameen's solution was group lending. Borrowers were organised into small groups, and if one member failed to repay, the others would lose access to future loans. This gave members a strong incentive to choose reliable partners and to support each other, effectively replacing physical security with social pressure.

The results appeared extraordinary. Grameen reported repayment rates of over 95 per cent, higher than many commercial banks, and the great majority of its borrowers were women, who were seen as more likely to invest in their families. By the early 2000s, microfinance institutions were serving tens of millions of people worldwide, and in 2006 Yunus and the Grameen Bank were jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. Microfinance was widely promoted as a powerful tool for ending poverty, one that, unlike traditional aid, paid for itself.

Yet as the movement grew, doubts began to emerge. Most early evidence of success came from stories of individual borrowers, which, however inspiring, could not show whether microfinance made a difference on average. Between 2009 and 2015, researchers carried out a series of randomised controlled trials in six countries, comparing areas where microfinance was introduced with similar areas where it was not. The results were sobering. Access to microcredit allowed some people to start or expand businesses, but on average it did not significantly increase household incomes, and there was little evidence that it improved health, education or women's empowerment.

Other problems emerged as microfinance became a commercial industry. In some countries, lenders competed aggressively, and many borrowers took out several loans at once, using one to repay another. In the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh in 2010, a crisis of over-indebtedness led to protests, mass defaults and reports of borrowers driven to desperation by aggressive collection practices. The state government responded by severely restricting microfinance lenders, and the industry there collapsed.

None of this means that microfinance has failed. In my view, the problem lies less in microfinance itself than in the inflated expectations that were attached to it. The trials found that loans did help people to manage irregular incomes, cope with emergencies and buy items such as roofs or livestock that would otherwise have been out of reach. Those are real benefits, even if they fall short of lifting people out of poverty. It is also worth noting that the most successful entrepreneurs in the trials did grow their businesses substantially; the average simply concealed their success.

Researchers have also found that other financial services may matter as much as loans. Many poor households have a greater need for safe places to save money than for credit, and mobile banking has transformed access to savings and payments in countries such as Kenya, where millions of people now send and receive money by phone. The lesson of microfinance, perhaps, is not that small loans cannot help the poor, but that no single tool is likely to solve a problem as complex as poverty.

listening.scriptTitle: Ordering food for an office party
listening.script:
Narrator: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a catering company to order food for an office party. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.
Caterer: Good morning, Fresh Table Catering, this is Amy. How can I help?
Customer: Hi, Amy. I'd like to order food for our office party next month.
Caterer: Lovely. Let me start an order form. Can I have the name of your company?
Customer: Yes, it's Brightline Design.
Caterer: Brightline Design. And your name?
Customer: Peter Gallagher. That's G, A, double L, A, G, H, E, R.
Caterer: Thank you, Peter. What's the date of the party?
Customer: Friday the twenty-first of November.
Caterer: And how many guests are you expecting?
Customer: We've got about forty staff, and we've invited some clients, so it'll be around fifty-five.
Caterer: Fifty-five people. Will it be a sit-down meal or a buffet?
Customer: A buffet, I think. People will want to move around and chat.
Caterer: Fine. And where will it be held? At your office?
Customer: No, our office is too small. We've hired the function room at the Riverside Hotel. It's on Canal Street.
Caterer: I know it well. And what time would you like the food delivered?
Customer: The party starts at seven, so could you deliver at half past six?
Caterer: Certainly.
Narrator: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.
Caterer: Now, we have three buffet menus. The Classic menu is sandwiches, salads and fruit. That's twelve pounds a head. The Deluxe menu adds hot dishes, such as curries and pasta, for eighteen pounds a head. And the Premium menu includes a carving station with a chef, at twenty-six pounds.
Customer: I think the Deluxe would be best. The Premium is more than our budget allows.
Caterer: Good choice. Do any of your guests have special dietary needs?
Customer: Yes, we have four vegetarians and two people who can't eat gluten.
Caterer: No problem. We'll label all the dishes clearly. Would you like us to provide drinks?
Customer: No, the hotel is providing those.
Caterer: And what about staff to serve the food? We can provide two waiters for the evening.
Customer: I don't think we need them for a buffet. But could you supply the plates and cutlery? The hotel charges a lot for theirs.
Caterer: Yes, that's included in the price. We'll collect everything the next morning.
Customer: Great. And how do I pay?
Caterer: We ask for a deposit of twenty per cent when you confirm the booking, and the rest within fourteen days of the event.
Narrator: That is the end of Part 1.

listening.scriptTitle: A visit to an organic farm
listening.script:
Narrator: Part 2. You will hear a guide talking to a group of visitors at an organic farm. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
Guide: Morning, everyone, and welcome to Hollybrook Farm. I'm Joe, and I'll be showing you round today. The farm has been in my family for four generations, but it's only been organic for the last fifteen years.
Guide: People often ask why we converted. It wasn't because of the higher prices organic food can fetch, although that helps. My father had noticed that the number of birds on the farm had fallen dramatically, and he became convinced that the chemicals we were using were to blame. Within five years of stopping, many species had returned.
Guide: Being organic isn't easy, though. The hardest part for us isn't the paperwork or the inspections, it's controlling weeds without chemicals. We use machines and a lot of manual labour, and in a wet summer it can feel like a losing battle.
Guide: You'll notice we don't grow the same crop in a field two years running. We use a five-year rotation, and the key year is the one where we grow clover. Clover takes nitrogen from the air and puts it into the soil, so it does the job that chemical fertiliser would otherwise do.
Guide: We sell most of our produce directly to customers through a weekly vegetable box scheme. We used to supply a supermarket, but they kept pushing the price down, so we stopped three years ago. The box scheme now has about six hundred customers.
Guide: Just a couple of safety points before we go. Please keep to the paths, and don't feed the animals. They're on carefully controlled diets.
Narrator: Now look at questions 16 to 20.
Guide: Let me explain the route we'll take. We start here at the farmyard, and we'll head first to the old barn, which we've converted into a farm shop and café. You'll be able to taste our cheese there at the end of the tour.
Guide: From there, we'll walk down to the orchard, where we grow apples and pears. That's also where we keep our bees, which pollinate the fruit trees. Don't worry, the hives are fenced off.
Guide: Next to the orchard is the dairy, where the cows are milked twice a day. If we're lucky, we'll arrive in time to see the afternoon milking.
Guide: Beyond the dairy, there's the wildlife pond, which we dug ten years ago. It's become home to frogs, newts and dragonflies, and it's where the school groups do most of their nature studies.
Guide: And finally, on the hill, there's the wind turbine, which generates about half the electricity the farm uses. There's a viewing platform beside it with the best view of the whole farm, so it's a good place to finish before we come back down for the cheese.
Narrator: That is the end of Part 2.

listening.scriptTitle: Designing an app for older people
listening.script:
Narrator: Part 3. You will hear two computer science students, Kevin and Grace, discussing their app design project with their tutor. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.
Tutor: So, remind me what your app is for.
Grace: It's an app to help older people remember to take their medication. Lots of older people take several different medicines every day, and it's easy to forget a dose or take one twice.
Tutor: And how did you research what users need?
Kevin: We were going to send out an online survey, but we realised that the people who most need the app are the least likely to answer online surveys. So we visited a community centre and talked to people face to face.
Tutor: That was a wise decision. What did you learn?
Grace: The biggest surprise was that most of them didn't want lots of features. We'd planned to include a health diary and video calls with doctors, but they said that would make it confusing. They just wanted something simple and reliable.
Kevin: And several people said that small text on phones is a real problem, so we've made the font size adjustable.
Tutor: Good. How are you handling the reminders themselves?
Grace: That was a difficult decision. A sound alone is easy to miss if you're in another room, so the app also sends a message to a family member if a dose hasn't been confirmed after thirty minutes.
Tutor: Did people have any concerns about that?
Kevin: A few were worried it might feel like being watched. So we made it optional. Users choose whether to turn it on.
Tutor: That seems a sensible balance. And what's your plan for testing?
Grace: We'd like to give the app to ten people from the community centre for two weeks and interview them afterwards.
Tutor: Two weeks might not be long enough to see if people keep using it. I'd suggest at least a month.
Narrator: Now look at questions 26 to 30.
Tutor: Let's go through the design decisions you still need to make. I've got some comments on each. First, the colour scheme.
Kevin: We've used pale blue and grey.
Tutor: The contrast is too low. Older users often have weaker eyesight, so you need much stronger contrast, dark text on a light background.
Grace: What about the buttons?
Tutor: They're too close together. People with less steady hands will press the wrong one. Make them bigger and put more space between them.
Kevin: And the icons? We designed our own.
Tutor: They're attractive, but I'm not sure users will understand them. Add a word under each icon.
Grace: The settings menu is quite long.
Tutor: That's fine for now. Most users will only open it once, when a family member sets up the app.
Kevin: And the instructions? We've written a user guide.
Tutor: Try making a short video instead. Your interviews suggested people found written instructions hard to follow.
Narrator: That is the end of Part 3.

listening.script:
Narrator: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about how scientists monitor volcanoes. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
Lecturer: Good afternoon. Around eight hundred million people live within a hundred kilometres of an active volcano, so predicting eruptions is a matter of life and death. Today I'll describe the main methods volcanologists use and some of their limitations.
Lecturer: The most important tool is the seismometer, which records ground vibrations. Before an eruption, magma forces its way up through the rock, breaking it as it rises, and this produces swarms of small earthquakes. A sudden increase in the number of these earthquakes is often the first warning sign. Most dangerous volcanoes now have a network of seismometers around them, transmitting data in real time.
Lecturer: The second method measures changes in the shape of the volcano. As magma collects beneath it, the ground swells, rather like a balloon being inflated. These changes may be only a few centimetres, but they can be measured very precisely using GPS receivers fixed to the ground, and from space using satellites with radar.
Lecturer: Third, scientists monitor gases. As magma rises, gases dissolved in it, especially sulphur dioxide, escape through cracks in the ground. A sharp rise in sulphur dioxide can indicate that fresh magma is approaching the surface. Collecting samples used to be extremely dangerous, but today much of this work is done by drones, which can fly directly through the gas clouds.
Lecturer: Fourth, there's temperature. Satellites with thermal cameras can detect hot spots on the surface, and changes in the temperature of crater lakes can also be significant.
Lecturer: Now, a success story. In 1991, Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines produced one of the largest eruptions of the twentieth century. Monitoring had begun only two months before, but scientists recognised the warning signs and persuaded the authorities to evacuate tens of thousands of people. It's estimated that at least five thousand lives were saved.
Lecturer: But prediction remains far from perfect. Some volcanoes show warning signs for months or even years and then don't erupt at all. If authorities evacuate an area and nothing happens, people may be less willing to leave the next time, a problem known as warning fatigue. Other volcanoes give very little warning. In 2014, Mount Ontake in Japan erupted with almost no warning, killing sixty-three hikers who were near the summit. That eruption was driven by steam rather than magma, which makes it much harder to detect.
Lecturer: Increasingly, researchers are using machine learning to analyse the vast amounts of data from monitoring networks, looking for patterns that humans might miss. It's an exciting development, but these systems need records of past eruptions to learn from, and for many volcanoes those records are very limited.
Narrator: That is the end of Part 4.

reading.passage:
Glass is so common today that it is easy to forget how remarkable a material it is: hard yet transparent, made from some of the most ordinary substances on Earth. Its main ingredient is silica, the chief component of sand, which melts at around 1,700 degrees Celsius. By adding other materials, glassmakers can lower this temperature considerably, making the process far more practical.

Natural glass has existed for millions of years. When lightning strikes sand, or when volcanic lava cools very quickly, it can form glass. Obsidian, a dark volcanic glass, was used by early humans to make extremely sharp tools and arrowheads, and it was traded over long distances in prehistoric times. The first man-made glass, however, appeared in Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq, around 3,500 years ago. At first it was used to make beads and other small decorative objects, which were treated as luxury items, comparable in value to precious stones.

For the next 1,500 years, making glass vessels was a slow and difficult process. Craftsmen formed the hot glass around a core made of clay and dung, and then removed the core once the glass had cooled. The resulting bottles were small, and they were mainly used to hold expensive perfumes and oils. Everything changed in the first century BC, when glassmakers somewhere along the eastern coast of the Mediterranean discovered that molten glass could be inflated by blowing into it through a long tube. Glassblowing made it possible to produce vessels quickly, in a wide range of shapes and sizes, and glass became affordable for ordinary people throughout the Roman Empire.

The Romans also began to use glass in windows, although Roman window glass was thick and only partly transparent. For many centuries, clear glass remained difficult to produce, because impurities in the raw materials gave it a green or brown tint. In fifteenth-century Venice, glassmakers on the island of Murano developed a nearly colourless glass known as cristallo, by carefully purifying their ingredients. The Venetian government valued the industry so highly that glassmakers were forbidden from leaving the republic, in order to protect their secrets. Some escaped nevertheless, and the knowledge gradually spread across Europe.

Glass also transformed science. Lenses, made by grinding glass into curved shapes, were used in spectacles from the late thirteenth century, extending the working lives of scholars and craftsmen whose eyesight was failing. In the early seventeenth century, lenses made possible the invention of both the telescope and the microscope. With his telescope, Galileo observed the moons of Jupiter, while early microscopes revealed for the first time the existence of bacteria and cells. Glass laboratory equipment, which does not react with most chemicals, was equally essential to the development of modern chemistry.

Producing large sheets of flat glass remained a challenge until the twentieth century. Earlier methods involved blowing a large cylinder or disc and then flattening it, which produced uneven glass with visible distortions. In the 1950s, the British engineer Alastair Pilkington invented the float process, in which molten glass is poured onto a bath of liquid tin. The glass spreads out and floats on the tin, forming a perfectly flat, smooth surface without any need for grinding or polishing. Today almost all the world's flat glass is made this way, from car windscreens to the glass walls of skyscrapers.

Glass continues to evolve. Optical fibres, thin strands of extremely pure glass, carry the light signals that transmit most of the world's internet data. The screens of smartphones are protected by chemically strengthened glass that resists scratches and cracks. And because glass can be recycled repeatedly without any loss of quality, it is likely to remain an important material in a world increasingly concerned with sustainability.

reading.passage:
A  Octopuses have long fascinated scientists because they seem to break the rules about where intelligence is found. Most animals that show complex problem-solving, such as apes, dolphins and crows, are vertebrates with long lives and rich social lives. Octopuses are molluscs, more closely related to snails and clams than to any mammal. Most species live for only one or two years, and they spend almost their entire lives alone. Yet they are capable of behaviour that, in a mammal, would be regarded as clear evidence of intelligence.

B  Stories of octopuses escaping from aquariums are common, and many are well documented. Octopuses have no bones, so they can squeeze through any gap larger than their beak, the only hard part of their body. In one famous case at an aquarium in New Zealand, an octopus named Inky escaped from its tank at night, crossed the floor and slid down a drainpipe that led to the sea. In laboratories, octopuses have learned to unscrew the lids of jars to reach food inside, and some have learned to do so from the inside of a closed jar.

C  Perhaps the most striking evidence of their intelligence is their use of tools. In 2009, researchers in Indonesia filmed veined octopuses collecting coconut shells discarded by people, carrying them across the sea floor, sometimes for considerable distances, and assembling them into shelters when threatened. What makes this behaviour significant is that the octopuses carried the shells before they needed them, an apparent sign of planning that was previously thought to be limited to a small number of animals.

D  The structure of the octopus nervous system is very different from ours. An octopus has around 500 million neurons, roughly as many as a dog, but about two thirds of them are located not in its brain but in its eight arms. Each arm can taste, touch and respond to its surroundings with a high degree of independence. An arm that has been separated from the body will continue to reach for food and try to pass it towards where the mouth would be. Some researchers describe the octopus as having a central brain that sets general goals, while the arms work out the details for themselves.

E  Octopuses are also masters of disguise. Their skin contains thousands of special cells that can change colour in a fraction of a second, and they can alter the texture of their skin to resemble rock or seaweed. The mimic octopus goes further, imitating the shapes and movements of other, more dangerous animals, such as lionfish and sea snakes. Strangely, octopuses appear to be colour-blind, and how they match their surroundings so precisely remains something of a mystery. One theory is that light-sensitive proteins in the skin itself may help them to detect colour.

F  Why did such intelligence evolve in short-lived, solitary animals? One widely accepted explanation is that the ancestors of octopuses lost their protective shells. Without a shell, they became vulnerable to predators, but they also gained the ability to move freely and to explore new environments. Survival came to depend on flexible behaviour: finding hiding places, hunting a wide range of prey and outwitting predators. Intelligence, on this view, was the price of giving up armour.

G  The growing recognition of octopus intelligence has ethical consequences. In 2021, a review commissioned by the British government concluded that octopuses, along with crabs and lobsters, are sentient, meaning that they can experience pain and pleasure. As a result, they were included in animal welfare legislation in the United Kingdom. The findings have also fuelled opposition to plans for commercial octopus farming, which critics argue would cause great suffering to animals that are curious, solitary and easily bored.

reading.passage:
Boredom has a poor reputation. It is associated with wasted time, restlessness and, in children, bad behaviour. Surveys suggest that it is one of the most commonly experienced emotions, particularly among teenagers, and that people will go to considerable lengths to avoid it. In one widely reported experiment, participants were left alone in a room for fifteen minutes with nothing to do except press a button that gave them a mild electric shock. A quarter of the women and two thirds of the men chose to shock themselves at least once rather than simply sit with their thoughts.

Today, of course, few people need to experience boredom at all. Smartphones offer an endless supply of entertainment that can fill every spare moment: the queue at the supermarket, the wait for a bus, the minutes before falling asleep. Many people reach for their phones at the first hint of boredom, often without being aware they are doing so. Some psychologists have begun to ask whether this constant stimulation comes at a cost, and whether boredom, unpleasant as it is, might serve a useful purpose.

One argument is that boredom acts as a signal. Just as pain warns us of physical harm, boredom tells us that our current activity is not satisfying our needs and that we should look for something more meaningful to do. On this view, boredom is not a problem in itself but a prompt to change direction. The difficulty is that the quick fix of a phone silences the signal without addressing its cause. We stop feeling bored, but we do not necessarily find anything more worthwhile to do.

A second argument concerns creativity. In a study published in 2014, participants who had first spent fifteen minutes copying numbers from a telephone directory, a deliberately dull task, then produced more creative ideas when asked to think of uses for a pair of plastic cups than participants who had not done the boring task. The researchers suggested that boredom encourages the mind to wander, and that mind-wandering allows unexpected connections to form. Other studies have produced similar results, although critics point out that the effects are small and that the tasks used in laboratories bear little resemblance to real creative work.

I am inclined to think that the creativity argument has been somewhat overstated in popular accounts. Not all boredom is productive. Chronic boredom, the kind experienced by people trapped in monotonous jobs or in prison, is associated with depression, anxiety and risky behaviour, and there is nothing romantic about it. The kind of boredom that may be valuable is brief and occasional: the empty half-hour that leaves space for reflection, rather than months of meaningless routine.

What does this mean for children? Many parents feel under pressure to fill their children's time with organised activities and to rescue them from boredom whenever it appears. Some educational researchers argue that this may be a mistake. Children who learn to cope with periods of unstructured time, they suggest, develop the ability to entertain themselves, to invent games and to pursue their own interests. Teachers have reported that some children become distressed when asked to sit quietly without a screen, which may indicate that this ability is becoming less common, although systematic evidence is limited.

None of this means that we should seek out boredom for its own sake, or throw away our phones. But it may be worth resisting the reflex to fill every pause. The next time you find yourself waiting with nothing to do, it might be worth leaving your phone in your pocket, at least for a few minutes, and seeing where your thoughts lead.

listening.script:
Narrator: Part 3. You will hear some conversations between two or more people. You will be asked to answer three questions about what the speakers say in each conversation.
Narrator: Conversation 1.
Woman: Hi, this is Sandra from the marketing department. I'm in conference room B, and the projector isn't showing anything from my laptop. My presentation starts in fifteen minutes.
Man: Have you tried the cable that comes out of the wall? The one on the table was damaged last week, and we haven't replaced it yet.
Woman: Oh, I didn't know that. I've been using the one on the table.
Man: Try the wall connection. If that doesn't work, I'll bring a spare projector up from the IT office. It'll only take me five minutes.
Narrator: Conversation 2.
Man: Good evening, Bellini's Restaurant.
Woman B: Hi, I'd like to book a table for eight people this Friday at seven thirty. It's for a colleague's retirement dinner.
Man: I'm sorry, we're fully booked at seven thirty. We could seat you at six or at nine.
Woman B: Nine is too late for some of our guests. Six will be fine. Also, could we have a private room? There'll be a few speeches.
Man: Our private room holds up to ten people, so that's no problem. There is a fifty-dollar booking fee for it, though.
Narrator: Conversation 3.
Woman: Mark, the shipment of printer cartridges still hasn't arrived. The supplier said it would be here on Tuesday.
Man B: I called them this morning. Apparently there's been a problem at the port, and everything's held up.
Woman: We're almost out, and the accounting team needs to print the annual reports this week.
Man B: Well, the office supply store on Main Street is open until eight.
Narrator: Conversation 4.
Man: Thanks for coming in, Ms. Okada. This is my colleague, David Chen, who manages our design team.
Man B: Nice to meet you. I was very impressed by your portfolio, especially the packaging you designed for that tea company.
Woman: Thank you. That was one of my favorite projects.
Man B: This position involves a lot of work with clients. Can you tell us about a time when a client disagreed with your ideas?
Woman: Sure. Last year a client rejected my first three designs, so I invited them to a workshop where we sketched ideas together. They loved the final version.
Man: That's exactly the kind of approach we're looking for. We'll be making a decision by the end of next week.
Narrator: Conversation 5.
Woman B: Hi, I'm calling about my flight to Singapore next Thursday. I need to come back a day later than planned.
Man: Let me check. Yes, there's a seat on the Saturday evening flight. There's a change fee of seventy-five dollars, though.
Woman B: That's fine, my company will cover it. Could you also check whether there's an aisle seat available?
Man: I'm afraid the aisle seats are all taken, but I can put you in an exit row. Those seats have extra legroom.
Narrator: Conversation 6.
Man B: Have you heard? We're moving to the new building on Harbor Road in March.
Woman: Really? That's great news. This office is far too crowded.
Man B: The new one is a lot bigger. But it's nowhere near the train station, so a lot of us will have a longer commute.
Woman: Maybe the company will provide a shuttle bus. I'll ask about it at Friday's staff meeting.
Narrator: Conversation 7.
Woman: The proposal for the new website looks great, but the cost is almost twice what we budgeted.
Man: I know. The designer included an online store, which we didn't originally ask for.
Woman: Well, we've been talking about selling online for years.
Man: True. Should I ask her for a version without the store, so we can compare the prices?
Woman: Yes, please. And ask her how soon she could start.
Narrator: Conversation 8.
Man: Hi, I reserved a compact car for this afternoon. The name's Patel.
Woman B: Yes, Mr. Patel. Unfortunately, our compact cars weren't returned on time today, so we don't have one available. But we can give you a midsize car at no extra charge.
Man: That's fine. Would it be possible to return it at the airport location instead of here?
Woman B: Yes, but there's a twenty-dollar fee for returning it to a different location.
Narrator: Conversation 9.
Woman: OK, the launch event for our new wireless headphones is in two weeks. Jun, how are the invitations going?
Man: I sent them to about two hundred journalists and bloggers. Around sixty have replied so far.
Woman C: That's fewer than we hoped. Maybe we should offer them a chance to try the headphones before the event.
Woman: Good idea. Let's send review samples to everyone who confirms by Friday.
Narrator: Conversation 10.
Man B: Hi, this is Tom in apartment 4C. The heating in my bedroom hasn't worked since last night.
Woman: I'm sorry to hear that. Our maintenance technician is fully booked today. I could send him tomorrow morning.
Man B: It's supposed to drop below freezing tonight.
Woman: Let me see what I can do. I'll call an outside repair company and get back to you within the hour.
Narrator: Conversation 11.
Woman B: Hello, I'm calling from Greenleaf Café. We'd like to order more of your paper cups, but a larger quantity this time, about ten thousand.
Man: Certainly. For orders over five thousand, we offer a ten percent discount.
Woman B: Great. Could you also print our logo on them?
Man: Yes, but custom printing adds two weeks to the delivery time.
Woman B: That should be OK. Our current supply will last about a month.
Narrator: Conversation 12. Look at the floor directory.
Woman: Excuse me, I have a two o'clock appointment with Ms. Rivera in Human Resources.
Man: Ah, Human Resources moved last week. They swapped floors with the legal department, but the directory hasn't been updated yet.
Woman: Thanks for letting me know. Is the elevator over there?
Man: Yes, but it's being serviced this afternoon, so you'll have to take the stairs, I'm afraid.
Narrator: Conversation 13. Look at the price list.
Man B: Hi, I need flyers printed for our store's grand opening. How soon could you do a thousand?
Woman B: We could have them ready by Thursday.
Man B: The opening is on Wednesday morning, so I'd need them by Tuesday at the latest.
Woman B: We can do that with our rush service, which costs an extra twenty dollars.
Man B: OK, let's do that.

listening.script:
Narrator: Part 4. You will hear some talks given by a single speaker. You will be asked to answer three questions about what the speaker says in each talk.
Narrator: Talk 1.
Woman: Hello, this message is for Mr. Daniel Ross. This is Kelly from Brightsmile Dental Clinic. I'm calling about your appointment this Thursday at ten a.m. Unfortunately, Dr. Hayes will be attending a conference that day, so we need to reschedule. We have openings on Friday morning or on Monday afternoon. Please call us back at your earliest convenience to choose a time. Also, a reminder that our clinic has moved to the third floor of the same building, so please use the elevators on the left side of the lobby. Thank you.
Narrator: Talk 2.
Man B: Attention passengers on Pacific Air flight two-forty to Vancouver. The departure gate for this flight has been changed from gate twelve to gate thirty-one. Gate thirty-one is located in Terminal B, which can be reached by the airport train. Please allow at least fifteen minutes to get there. Boarding will begin at four fifteen, as originally scheduled. Passengers who require assistance should speak to a member of staff at the information desk next to gate twelve.
Narrator: Talk 3.
Woman B: Good morning, this is Lisa Grant with your traffic update on City Radio. Drivers heading downtown on Highway nine should expect delays of up to thirty minutes this morning because of road repairs near the river bridge. One lane is closed until noon. If you can, take Elm Street instead. Also, remember that the city marathon takes place this Sunday, and several streets in the city center will be closed from six a.m. to two p.m. Up next, we'll have the weather forecast for the weekend.
Narrator: Talk 4.
Man: Good afternoon, shoppers, and thank you for choosing Greenway Home Store. For the next two hours only, all kitchen appliances are thirty percent off, including coffee makers, toasters and blenders. And if you sign up for our free rewards card today at the customer service desk, you'll receive an additional ten percent off your entire purchase. Don't forget, we now offer free delivery on all orders over one hundred dollars. Happy shopping!
Narrator: Talk 5.
Woman C: Welcome to the Barton Chocolate Factory. My name's Maria, and I'll be your guide today. Our tour lasts about an hour. First, we'll see where the cocoa beans are roasted, and then we'll watch our chocolatiers at work. Now, I know what you're all waiting for. Yes, there will be samples. Before we start, please put on the hairnets in the basket by the door. They're required in all production areas. And please note that photography isn't permitted inside the factory, to protect our recipes. At the end of the tour, you'll have a chance to visit our gift shop.
Narrator: Talk 6.
Man B: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the third annual Small Business Growth Conference. It's my pleasure to introduce our first speaker, Dr. Angela Moore. Dr. Moore founded a software company in her garage fifteen years ago, and today it employs over five hundred people. She's also the author of the best-selling book Starting Small. This morning, she'll share her advice on how small companies can compete with much larger ones. After her talk, there'll be time for questions, so please write yours on the cards on your tables. Please join me in welcoming Dr. Moore.
Narrator: Talk 7.
Woman: In business news today, the Swedish furniture retailer Nordhem has announced that it will acquire Comfort Living, a chain of home furnishing stores with more than eighty locations across the country. The deal is expected to be completed by the end of the year. Nordhem's chief executive said the acquisition will allow the company to expand its presence in smaller cities, where it currently has no stores. Analysts say the move will make Nordhem the largest furniture seller in the region. Comfort Living stores will keep their name for at least two years.
Narrator: Talk 8.
Man: Before we finish today's meeting, I want to mention a change to how we handle travel expenses. Starting next month, all expense reports must be submitted through the new online system instead of on paper. You'll need to upload photos of your receipts, so please don't throw them away. The finance team will hold two training sessions next week, on Tuesday and Thursday at three p.m. I know some of you are worried about the new system, but I tried it last week, and it took me less than five minutes. Please sign up for one of the sessions by Friday.
Narrator: Talk 9. Look at the weather forecast.
Woman B: Hi, everyone. As you know, our company picnic is planned for this week at Lakeside Park. I've just checked the forecast, and unfortunately it's going to rain on Tuesday, which was our original date. So we're moving it to the day after the rain, when it's supposed to be sunny. Food will be provided, but please bring your own drinks. And if you'd like to join the volleyball tournament, add your name to the list in the break room by tomorrow.
Narrator: Talk 10. Look at the schedule.
Man B: Good morning, and welcome to today's marketing workshop. Before we begin, there's one change to the schedule. Mark Davis's flight was delayed this morning, so he won't be able to give his talk on social media strategy at ten thirty. Instead, he'll take the last slot of the morning, and the panel discussion will move to ten thirty. Lisa Wong's session on marketing trends will go ahead as planned. Lunch will be served in the main hall at twelve thirty.

CITY TO EXPAND BIKE-SHARING PROGRAM
Greenport — The city council voted on Tuesday to add 40 new bike-sharing stations over the next two years, bringing the total to 120. The expansion will focus on neighborhoods in the north and east of the city, which currently have few stations.
Since the program launched four years ago, the number of trips has grown every year, reaching 1.2 million last year. A survey found that nearly a third of users ride the bikes to and from train stations.
The expansion will be funded mainly through a sponsorship agreement with Velo Insurance, whose logo will appear on the bikes. Council member Diane Ortiz said the deal means "the program will not cost taxpayers anything extra."

passages.title: Article
passages.text:
Small Town, Big Screen
When the Palace Cinema in Millbrook closed in 2015, many residents feared the town had lost its only cinema for good. The building, which opened in 1932, sat empty for six years.
Then, in 2021, a group of local residents formed a cooperative to buy and restore it. More than 600 people each contributed at least $100, becoming co-owners of the cinema. Volunteers spent eighteen months repairing the roof, restoring the original seats and installing modern digital projectors.
The Palace reopened last spring and has exceeded expectations. Attendance has averaged 2,000 visitors a month, and the cinema now hosts film clubs, live music and children's workshops. "It's become the heart of the town again," said cooperative chair Helen Marsh.
The cooperative is now raising money to add a second, smaller screen, which would allow the cinema to show more independent films.

Greenfield Farmers' Market — New Location from May 1
The Greenfield Farmers' Market is moving from the parking lot on Station Road to Central Park, next to the fountain. The market will continue to run every Saturday from 8:00 A.M. to 1:00 P.M. The new location offers more space, shade from the trees and better access for wheelchairs. Vendors interested in a stall should apply to the market coordinator, Ben Okoro, by April 10.

———

To: Ben Okoro
From: Lucy Hartman
Date: April 6
Subject: Stall application

Dear Mr. Okoro,
I run a small business making natural soaps and candles, and I would love to have a stall at the market in its new location. I have sold my products at craft fairs for several years, but this would be my first farmers' market. I would need a stall near an electrical outlet, as I like to demonstrate how my candles are made using a small heater. Could you let me know whether this is possible?
Best wishes,
Lucy Hartman, Hartman Naturals

———

Market Thrives in New Home — Greenfield Gazette, June 2
A month after moving to Central Park, the Greenfield Farmers' Market is attracting record crowds. Coordinator Ben Okoro estimates that visitor numbers have risen by 40 percent. The market now has 35 stalls, up from 22 last year. Among the newcomers is Hartman Naturals, whose candle-making demonstrations have become a favorite with children. "The shade makes a huge difference in summer," said vegetable grower Tom Reyes, who has sold at the market for ten years. The only complaint, Mr. Okoro admitted, is the lack of parking near the park, and organizers are discussing a shuttle bus from Station Road.

listening.script:
Narrator: Part 4. You will hear some talks given by a single speaker. You will be asked to answer three questions about what the speaker says in each talk.
Narrator: Talk 1.
Man: Hi, Ms. Larson, this is Rick from Fairview Auto Repair. I'm calling about your car. We've finished the oil change and replaced the front brakes, so the car is safe to drive. However, the part we need to fix the air conditioning hasn't arrived yet. The supplier says it should be here by Thursday. You can either pick up the car today and bring it back on Thursday, or leave it with us until then. Please give me a call at five-five-five, zero one four four to let me know.
Narrator: Talk 2.
Woman B: Attention, visitors. The Hartley Museum of Art will close in thirty minutes. Please make your way toward the main exit. If you rented an audio guide, please return it to the desk next to the coat check. Our gift shop will remain open for an additional fifteen minutes after the galleries close. And don't forget that our new exhibition of Japanese prints opens next Saturday. Members can attend a special preview on Friday evening.
Narrator: Talk 3.
Man B: Do you want to speak a new language with confidence? At Lingua Plus, our small classes have no more than six students, so you'll get plenty of chances to practice. All our teachers are native speakers, and classes are available mornings, evenings and weekends. This month only, new students who sign up for a ten-week course will receive a free online dictionary subscription. Visit our Web site to take a free placement test and find the right class for you.
Narrator: Talk 4.
Woman C: Welcome aboard the Harbor Lights boat tour. Over the next hour, we'll travel along the coast and past the old lighthouse, and you'll get great views of the city skyline. Now, the wind is quite strong out on the water today, so you might want to hold on to your hats. Snacks and drinks are available at the counter on the lower deck. And please remember to stay seated while the boat is moving.
Narrator: Talk 5.
Man: Good morning, everyone. I want to update you on a security change. Starting Monday, the main entrance will have new electronic badge readers, and the old paper visitor passes will no longer be used. All employees will need to scan their badges to enter the building. If your badge isn't working, please visit the security office in the lobby before Friday so we can fix it. Visitors will now be registered online by the person they're meeting.
Narrator: Talk 6.
Woman: And now for the weather. It'll be a cloudy morning across the region, with temperatures around fifteen degrees. Heavy rain is expected to arrive in the afternoon and continue through the evening, so if you're planning to drive home from work, allow extra time. Tomorrow will be much brighter, with sunshine all day and highs of twenty-two. The weekend looks warm and dry, perfect for the Riverside Food Festival on Saturday.
Narrator: Talk 7.
Man B: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for joining us for our annual awards dinner. It's my great pleasure to present this year's Employee of the Year award to Sofia Martinez from our customer service team. Over the past year, Sofia trained eight new team members and helped reduce customer waiting times by almost half. Many of the customers she helped took the time to write letters of thanks, and several of them are in the folder I'm holding. Sofia, please come up to the stage.
Narrator: Talk 8.
Woman B: Welcome back to Business Today. My guest this week is Jonathan Reed, author of the new book The Four-Day Week. Jonathan spent two years studying companies that reduced their working week from five days to four without lowering salaries. He found that most of them saw no drop in productivity, and many reported that employees took fewer sick days. In the second half of the show, Jonathan will take questions from listeners, so call in with yours.
Narrator: Talk 9. Look at the discount table.
Woman C: Hello, shoppers! This weekend is our big spring sale at Maxwell's Department Store. Discounts depend on the floor. On the first floor, cosmetics are ten percent off. Clothing on the second floor is twenty percent off. Home goods on the third floor are thirty percent off. And electronics on the fourth floor are fifteen percent off. Today only, if you spend more than one hundred dollars on the third floor, you'll also get a free set of towels.
Narrator: Talk 10. Look at the chart.
Man: Thanks for coming, everyone. As you know, we asked our customers which part of our mobile app they'd most like us to improve. As you can see on the chart, the most common answer was search, followed by the checkout process. But we've decided to start with the second one, because problems there cause people to abandon their purchases, which costs us money directly. The design team will present some ideas at next Monday's meeting.

passages.title: Article
passages.text:
From Market Stall to Main Street
When Amara Osei started selling homemade hot sauce at a weekend market in 2016, she produced just twenty bottles a week in her kitchen. Today her company, Osei Spice, sells its sauces in more than 500 supermarkets across the country.
Ms. Osei, who previously worked as an accountant, says her financial background was essential. "I knew exactly how much each bottle cost to make, so I never sold at a loss," she explains. Her big break came in 2020, when a national supermarket chain discovered her products at a food fair.
The company now employs 45 people at a factory in Leeds. Next year, it plans to launch a range of cooking sauces and to begin exporting to Europe.

CITY LAUNCHES FOOD WASTE COLLECTION
Starting in April, households in Millford will receive a small brown bin for food waste, which will be collected every week alongside regular recycling. The food waste will be turned into compost and energy at a new facility near the airport. The city hopes the program will cut the amount of household waste sent to landfill by a quarter.

———

To the Editor,
I support the new food waste program, but I'm concerned about the bins. Ours is so small that it fills up in three days, and in warm weather it attracts flies. Larger bins, or collection twice a week in summer, would make a big difference.
Patricia Wells, Millford

———

Millford Food Waste Program – Resident Survey (June)
Satisfied with the program: 72%
Main complaints: bin too small (41%), smell (27%), missed collections (19%), other (13%)
The city council will consider changes at its July meeting.

listening.script:
Narrator: Part 4. You will hear some talks given by a single speaker. You will be asked to answer three questions about what the speaker says in each talk.
Narrator: Talk 1.
Woman: Hello, Mr. Grant, this is Julia from Horizon Travel. I'm calling about your trip to Lisbon next month. Unfortunately, the hotel you chose has informed us that it will be closed for renovations during your stay. I've found a similar hotel nearby, the Atlantic Plaza, at the same price, and it also includes breakfast. I've e-mailed you the details. If you're happy with it, please reply to the e-mail by Friday, and I'll confirm the booking.
Narrator: Talk 2.
Man B: Good evening, shoppers. Fresh Fields Supermarket will be closing in fifteen minutes. Please bring your final purchases to the checkout. Self-service checkouts will close five minutes before the store. And don't miss tomorrow's special event. From ten until two, our bakery team will be offering free samples of our new range of whole-grain breads near the main entrance. Thank you for shopping at Fresh Fields.
Narrator: Talk 3.
Man: Good morning, and welcome to your first day at Precision Components. Before you go onto the factory floor, there are a few safety rules you need to know. Safety glasses and steel-toed boots must be worn at all times in the production area. You'll find them in the lockers in the changing room. Also, if you hear the alarm, which is a long, continuous tone, leave the building through the nearest exit and gather in the parking lot. Now, let's watch a short video about operating the machines safely.
Narrator: Talk 4.
Woman B: In local news, the new Riverside Public Library will open its doors to the public on Saturday. The three-story building replaces the old library, which had served the community for more than sixty years. In addition to its book collection, the new library includes a recording studio and a computer lab with free classes for seniors. The opening ceremony begins at ten a.m., and the mayor will cut the ribbon. Free parking will be available all weekend.
Narrator: Talk 5.
Woman C: Thank you for calling Northern Power. Our offices are currently closed. Our regular hours are eight a.m. to six p.m., Monday through Friday. To report a power outage, press one. To pay your bill using our automated system, press two. For all other questions, please visit our Web site, where you can also chat with a customer service representative during business hours.
Narrator: Talk 6.
Man B: Welcome, everyone. I'm Greg, and I'll be showing you around the office this morning. This is the main work area, where most of you will sit. Desks aren't assigned, so you can choose a different one each day. Over here is the kitchen. There's a full kitchen with a fridge and a microwave, and on Fridays the company provides lunch for everyone, so you won't need to bring lunch that day. After the tour, you'll meet with your managers to set up your computers.
Narrator: Talk 7.
Woman: Let's begin today's meeting with the quarterly results. I'm happy to report that sales rose by twelve percent compared with the same period last year, mainly thanks to strong demand for our new line of outdoor furniture. However, shipping costs increased sharply, which reduced our profits. To deal with this, we'll start working with a new shipping company next month. I'd now like to ask Diane to present the marketing plan for the summer.
Narrator: Talk 8.
Man: Big news from Hartman Furniture! After thirty years on Main Street, we're moving to a larger showroom on Route 9. To make the move easier, everything in our Main Street store must go. That's right, all sofas, tables and beds are forty percent off until the end of the month. And because we want you to enjoy your new furniture right away, delivery is free on every purchase. Don't wait. Once it's gone, it's gone!
Narrator: Talk 9. Look at the departure board.
Woman B: Hi, team. This is Rachel. I'm at the station, and I'm afraid our nine fifteen train to Manchester has been canceled. The next train is the nine forty-five, but it's a slow train with many stops, so I suggest we take the one after that instead. It's a faster train and should still get us there before the client meeting at one. I'll buy the tickets now, so just meet me at the entrance to the platform ten minutes before it leaves.
Narrator: Talk 10. Look at the chart.
Man B: As you know, the company needs to reduce spending next year. I've looked at the budget for our department, which is shown on this chart. Staff costs are our biggest expense, but we can't change those. Instead, I'd like to cut the area where we spend the least, so we'll be holding more meetings online and fewer in person. I'm open to other suggestions, so please e-mail me your ideas by the end of the week.

passages.title: Article

FARM OPENS STORE IN TOWN CENTER
Greenacre Farm, which has supplied vegetables to local restaurants for over twenty years, opened its first retail store on High Street last week. The store sells fruit, vegetables, eggs and cheese, all produced on the farm or by neighboring farmers.
"Customers kept asking where they could buy our products," said owner Ruth Collins. "Now they don't have to drive out to the farm."
The store is open Tuesday to Sunday. Every Saturday morning, children can take part in a free cooking class using seasonal produce.

passages.title: Article
passages.text:
Restaurant Review: Saffron Table
Saffron Table, which opened in the former post office building on Bridge Road two months ago, serves modern Indian cuisine in a bright, elegant dining room. Chef Arjun Mehta previously worked at several well-known restaurants in London before returning to his hometown.
The highlight of our meal was the slow-cooked lamb, which was tender and full of flavor. Vegetarians are well served too; the spinach and paneer curry was excellent. Our only disappointment was the service, which was friendly but slow on a busy Friday night.
Prices are reasonable, with most main dishes under $20. Reservations are strongly recommended on weekends.

passages.title: E-mail, program and e-mail
passages.text:
To: Dr. Laura Benson
From: Conference Committee, National Nursing Conference
Date: January 10
Subject: Invitation to speak

Dear Dr. Benson,
We would be honored if you would give the opening talk at this year's National Nursing Conference in Denver on March 14. Your research on reducing patient stress in hospitals has been widely praised. Speakers receive free registration, two nights' accommodation and travel expenses.

———

National Nursing Conference – Program, March 14
9:00 A.M. – Opening talk: "Calm Care: Reducing Patient Stress" – Dr. Laura Benson
10:30 A.M. – Workshop: New Technology on the Ward – Dr. Samuel Price
1:00 P.M. – Panel: The Future of Home Nursing
3:00 P.M. – Closing remarks

———

To: Conference Committee
From: Dr. Laura Benson
Date: March 2
Subject: Change of plans

Dear Committee,
I'm afraid my flight to Denver on March 13 has been canceled, and the earliest flight I can get arrives at 10:00 A.M. on March 14. I would be happy to exchange places with Dr. Price if he agrees. Otherwise, I could join the afternoon panel instead.
Best regards,
Laura Benson

passages.title: Notice, survey results and e-mail
passages.text:
NOTICE TO ALL EMPLOYEES – Commuter Survey
Next year, Delmont Industries will move from the city center to the new Westgate Business Park, about 12 kilometers away. To help us plan transportation, please complete the short online commuter survey by May 31. The results will be shared with all staff in June.

———

Commuter Survey – Summary of Results (June 10)
How employees currently travel to work: Train 46% · Car 31% · Bus 15% · Bicycle 8%
Most requested support: A shuttle bus from Central Station (58%) · More parking (22%) · Secure bicycle storage (12%) · Flexible working hours (8%)
Management response: A free shuttle will run from Central Station every 15 minutes during peak hours. Covered bicycle storage will be built next to the main entrance.

———

To: Facilities Department
From: Owen Clarke
Date: June 14
Subject: Shuttle bus

Hello,
Thank you for sharing the survey results. I'm glad about the shuttle from Central Station, as I take the train every day. However, I often start work at 6:30 A.M. for the early shift. Will the shuttle be running at that time? If not, I may need to start driving to work.
Owen Clarke, Production Department

Narrator: Part 3. You will hear some conversations between two or more people. You will be asked to answer three questions about what the speakers say in each conversation.
Narrator: Conversation 1.
Woman: Hi, I'm calling to refill my prescription. My name is Anna Lopez.
Man: Let me check. I'm afraid your prescription has no refills left, so we'll need approval from your doctor.
Woman: Oh, I see. Could you contact her for me?
Man: Yes, I'll send a request now. It usually takes one business day. We'll send you a text message when it's ready to pick up.
Narrator: Conversation 2.
Man B: Have you looked at the quotes for the new staff uniforms?
Woman B: Yes. Clarke Textiles is the cheapest, but they need eight weeks to deliver.
Man B: That's too long. The new hotel opens in five weeks.
Woman B: Then Harbor Uniforms is the best option. They're a little more expensive, but they can deliver within a month.
Man B: Let's go with them. Can you place the order today?
Narrator: Conversation 3.
Woman: Thanks for showing us the office space. It's in a great location.
Man: Yes, it's right next to the subway station, and the rent includes cleaning and security.
Man B: It's a bit smaller than we need, though. We're planning to hire ten more people next year.
Man: There's another unit on the floor above that's the same size. It'll be available in March. You could rent both.
Woman: That might work. Could you send us the details for both units?
Narrator: Conversation 4.
Man: Hi, I'm interested in your photography course for beginners. Do I need my own camera?
Woman B: Yes, but any digital camera will do. Even a phone camera is fine for the first few lessons.
Man: Great. And is the teacher experienced?
Woman B: Well, I've been teaching the course for fifteen years.
Man: Oh, you're the teacher! Sorry, I didn't realize.
Narrator: Conversation 5.
Woman: Excuse me, my flight from Rome was delayed, and I missed my connection to Toronto.
Man B: I'm sorry to hear that. The next flight to Toronto leaves at eight this evening, and there are seats available. I'll rebook you now.
Woman: Thank you. That's a long wait, though.
Man B: Here's a voucher for a meal at any restaurant in the terminal, and you're welcome to use our lounge while you wait.
Narrator: Conversation 6.
Man: Have you finished the slides for the client presentation?
Woman: Almost. I just need to add last month's sales figures.
Man: The presentation's in an hour.
Woman: I know. They'll be ready in twenty minutes. Could you ask Ben to set up the projector in the meeting room?
Man: Sure, I'll go and find him now.
Narrator: Conversation 7.
Woman B: Hi, I saw the sign about the community garden. Are there any plots available?
Man: There are three left. Each one is four meters by four, and the fee is forty dollars for the season.
Woman B: That sounds reasonable. Are tools provided?
Man: Yes, there's a shed with shared tools, and water is free too. You'll just need to attend a short orientation on Saturday morning.
Narrator: Conversation 8.
Man B: Everything's ready for tomorrow's outdoor concert in the courtyard.
Woman: Have you seen the forecast?
Man B: No. Is it going to rain?
Woman: Heavy rain all afternoon. We should move it to the main hall.
Man B: OK. I'll let the musicians know and ask the maintenance team to set up the chairs inside.
Narrator: Conversation 9.
Woman: We've been getting a lot of complaints about late deliveries this month.
Man: That's because our courier company is short of drivers. They told us things should improve by the end of the month.
Woman C: In the meantime, could we give customers a discount code when their delivery is late?
Woman: Good idea. Let's offer ten percent off their next order. Mia, could you write an e-mail to the affected customers?
Woman C: Sure, I'll draft it this morning.
Narrator: Conversation 10.
Man: Hi, my laptop screen has stopped working. I bought it here eight months ago.
Woman B: It's still under the one-year warranty, so the repair will be free. We'll need to send it to our repair center, though, which takes about a week.
Man: A week? I need it for work.
Woman B: In that case, we can lend you a laptop while yours is being repaired.
Narrator: Conversation 11.
Woman: Hi, this is Karen from Delta Consulting. We have a conference at your hotel on Thursday, and I need to change our lunch order.
Man B: Of course. I see you've ordered lunch for sixty people.
Woman: Yes, but twelve more people have registered, so we'll need lunch for seventy-two.
Man B: No problem, I'll update the order. Do any of the new guests have dietary requirements?
Woman: Two are vegetarian. I'll e-mail you their names.
Narrator: Conversation 12. Look at the bus schedule.
Man: Excuse me, does this bus go to Harbor Park?
Woman: Yes, it's Route 8. But I'm afraid you've just missed the seven forty.
Man: I need to be there by nine for a job interview.
Woman: Then take the next one. It gets there with ten minutes to spare.
Narrator: Conversation 13. Look at the price list.
Woman B: Hi, I'd like to order lunch boxes for a team meeting tomorrow. Twenty boxes, please.
Man B: Sure. Which kind would you like?
Woman B: Something light, but not sandwiches. We had those last time. Let's do the salad boxes.
Man B: OK. We can deliver at noon. Is there anything else?
Woman B: Yes, could you include twenty bottles of water as well?

listening.script:
Narrator: Part 4. You will hear some talks given by a single speaker. You will be asked to answer three questions about what the speaker says in each talk.
Narrator: Talk 1.
Man B: Hello, this is a message for all tenants at Linden Court from building management. On Wednesday and Thursday of next week, workers will be cleaning the outside windows of the building. Please keep your windows closed on those days, and remove any items from your balconies, such as plants and chairs. The workers will be using ropes and platforms, so the courtyard will be closed to residents. We apologize for any inconvenience.
Narrator: Talk 2.
Woman B: Good afternoon, passengers. This is your conductor speaking. Because of a signal problem near Riverton station, we'll be stopping here for approximately fifteen minutes. We expect to arrive in Bristol about twenty minutes behind schedule. Passengers who need to make connections should speak to a member of staff when we arrive. In the meantime, the café car at the rear of the train is open, and hot drinks are half price for the rest of the journey.
Narrator: Talk 3.
Man: Tired of spending your weekends cleaning? Let Sparkle Home Services do it for you! Our professional cleaners use only eco-friendly products that are safe for children and pets. Choose a one-time deep clean or a regular weekly or monthly service. Book online today and get your first cleaning for just forty-nine dollars. And if you're not completely satisfied, we'll come back and clean again for free.
Narrator: Talk 4.
Woman C: Now, please gather around this display case. The instrument you see here is a violin made in Italy in 1715. It's one of only about five hundred violins made by this craftsman that still exist today. In fact, this is the only one of its kind in a public museum in North America. Because it's so fragile, it's played only once a year, at a special concert in December. Please don't use flash photography in this room. Let's move on to the next gallery.
Narrator: Talk 5.
Man B: Good morning, everyone. Before we start, I'd like to introduce Priya Shah, who joins us today as our new sales manager. Priya comes to us from Atlas Electronics, where she led a team that doubled the company's online sales in three years. She'll be meeting with each of you individually over the next two weeks to learn about your accounts. Priya, would you like to say a few words?
Narrator: Talk 6.
Woman: You're listening to Book Talk on WRCB Radio. This week's featured book is The Silent Harbor, the first novel by local author Daniel Cruz. It tells the story of a fishing village during a difficult winter, and critics have praised its beautiful descriptions of the sea. Mr. Cruz will be reading from the book and signing copies at Page One Bookstore on Saturday at three p.m. The event is free, but seats are limited, so please call the store to reserve a place.
Narrator: Talk 7.
Man: I have an announcement about parking. Starting on the first of next month, all employees who park in the company garage will need a new parking permit. The old green permits will no longer be accepted. You can pick up the new blue permits from the reception desk, but you'll need to bring your employee ID card and your vehicle registration number. Permits are still free of charge. Please make sure you have yours before the end of this month.
Narrator: Talk 8.
Woman B: Welcome to this afternoon's workshop on time management. The first technique I want to share is simple. At the end of each workday, write down the three most important tasks for the next day. That's not as hard as it sounds. Most people can do it in under five minutes. The key is to start your morning with the first task on the list, before you check your e-mail. In a moment, I'll ask you to try this with a partner.
Narrator: Talk 9. Look at the floor plan.
Man: Hi, team. I just got the floor plan for next month's Home and Garden Expo. We originally requested the booth next to the main entrance, but it had already been taken. Instead, we've been given the booth beside the café, which should actually be great, because lots of people will stop there for a break. Please remember that setup begins at seven a.m. on the first day, and we need to be finished by nine, when the doors open.
Narrator: Talk 10. Look at the graph.
Woman C: Let's look at the number of visitors to our online store over the past six months. As you can see, the numbers were fairly steady at the start of the year. But in the month when we started our video advertising campaign, visits jumped sharply, and they've stayed high since then. Based on these results, we're going to increase our video advertising budget. I'd like the marketing team to suggest ideas for new videos by next Friday.

Atlas Motors Opens Plant in Ohio
Atlas Motors officially opened its new electric vehicle battery plant in Dayton, Ohio, on Tuesday. — [1] — The $800 million facility will employ 1,200 workers when it reaches full production next year. — [2] — Company officials said they chose Dayton because of its skilled workforce and its location close to several of the company's car factories. — [3] — The plant will also include a training center run in partnership with Dayton Community College. — [4] —

passages.title: Article
passages.text:
Designing for Everyday Life
Furniture designer Lena Holm is known for chairs and tables that are both beautiful and practical. Her latest collection, Nordic Home, uses wood from sustainably managed forests in Sweden, where she grew up.
"I design for small apartments," Ms. Holm explains. "Many young people live in limited space, so every piece should have more than one use." Her best-selling coffee table, for example, can be raised to become a dining table.
After studying architecture in Stockholm, Ms. Holm worked for a large furniture company for eight years before starting her own studio in 2016. Her pieces are now sold in twelve countries. Next spring, she will open her first showroom in New York.

CITY CONSIDERS BIKE LANES ON MAIN STREET
The Brookfield City Council is considering a proposal to add protected bike lanes on Main Street. Supporters say the lanes would make cycling safer and reduce traffic. However, some business owners worry that removing 40 parking spaces would hurt their sales. The council will hear public comments at its meeting on May 14 before making a decision.

———

To: City Council
From: Grace Lin, Owner, Lin's Bakery
Date: May 8
Subject: Main Street bike lanes

Dear Council Members,
I'm writing to support the bike lanes. Many of my customers already arrive on foot or by bicycle, and I believe safer cycling would bring more people to Main Street. I would ask, however, that the council keep a few short-term parking spaces near the shops for deliveries. I plan to speak at the May 14 meeting.
Grace Lin

———
